history.title: Alien: Covenant
history.text: This movie is so bad it's not even funny. And I know you are supposed to do a little "suspension of disbelief" for entertainment sake, but here there so much nonsense that you have to be a true moron not to be disgusted by it. And it starts really, really bad when in the first sequence the authors make Weyland, supposedly a genial scientist, say " I refuse to believe that mankind is a random byproduct of molecular circumstances, no more than the result of mere biological chance". Now, every schoolboy who has payed attention in his biology class knows that chance has very little to do with biological evolution. Not even the dumbest creationists now try to pass biological evolution for a random process. The grunt work of evolution is done by reproduction and natural selection, not random chance. Random chance is only useful for opening new possibilities. Starting a movie with such a horrible scientific blunder is a disgrace. But, even if, like Weyland says, "there must be more", and humans were created by aliens, what about the aliens? Can we accept that they are the product of biological evolution, or we must find another race of aliens that seeded them, and then another, ad infinitum? :) ***** SPOILER ALERT ***** But let' s go back to the almost infinite chain of nonsense in this movie instead. 1) David is supposed to have ended the race that seeded the humans and then wanted to destroy them by simply reaching their planet with one of their ships, with no surveillance, nobody getting even slightly alarmed, and then dropping a biological weapon on what appears to be their only city ( and we are talking about a race capable of interstellar travel..) 2) David want to "improve" the aliens generated by the biological weapon making them need a queen, eggs, a biological host that they have to infect by jumping on it to reach his mouth, while initially they can just infect any host by flying in the air like spores and reaching their host without them even noticing. How is that an "improvement"??? 3) The colonist mother ship appears to be so vulnerable to "stellar flares" that it looks perfectly normal that they risk to go up in flames every time they need to recharge their batteries. 4) You are responsible for 2k lives on the ship, have a clear mission to reach an habitable planet who 's already been explored and deemed safe, but then receive a transmission of a john denver ( I am not kidding) song from another one, who 's totally unexplored, but a bit closer, so yeah why not, let' s abandon the original plan and go explore the other planet! 5) Of course once you land you go stumbling happily around without any protection from bacteria or viruses (or spores) just because the air appears breathable. And the fact that there's vegetation but no animal life does not alarm you one bit. 6) Once two crew members get manifestly horribly sick you bring them immediately on board. 7) Once in the med bay, one crew member lock the other inside with the sick and mutating one, leaving ample time for the alien to jump out from the guy's back, attack the locked in crew member, then comes back with a rifle, slips on blood, hurts her foot, shoots the ceiling, and lose the rifle. Then she gets another one, with which she proceeds to blow up the spaceship they used to come down from the mother ship. And you cannot help thinking: why do we need the aliens at all, these supposed specialist are perfectly capable of exterminating themselves if just left alone.. 8) Why would David be so fascinated by the "alien" race and consider them "perfect"? If he likes animals that have as only goal to eat and care for their queen, there' s plenty of insects on Earth that do that perfectly :) Or maybe he considers physical strength and predatory behaviour a sign of perfection? Why a highly intelligent life form would ever think that??? And on top of this steaming pile of bull**it: character development is non existent, the character are so flat and insignificant that it's a hard to keep track of how many of them there are, there is not even one who is even slightly memorable, and the whole plot is predictable and boring in every detail . Everything goes literally just as you expect. And for most of the time is just looks like a reboot of the first movie, just lamer but with up to date special effects. And actually a remake would have been a much better option than this pile of ...nonsense. All in all, if the goal was spending millions of dollars to completely ruin a movie franchise it's would have been really hard do a better job than this.

history.title: Meaning from Data: Statistics Made Clear
history.review_title: Required Viewing for the Well Educated...but watch out for the pseudo sciences..
history.text: Easy to follow and pleasant course, Michael Starbird is a first class teacher and presenter, extremely smart, but never "imposing" or pretentious, and always playful. It s just the right kind of person to transmit the joy, fun and interest of doing mathematics ... You will get a survey of the fundamental of statistics, but what is more important, a clear picture of how useful it is, and in how many different and "unexpected" fields.. and also about the traps and pitfalls that lie in interpreting too naively (or dishonestly) statistical results. I would say it's "required viewing for the well educated person". I would also have liked to see a little more math and derivations, I am sure they could have been done without scaring anyone away.. My only gripe is that prof. Starbird gives social sciences and psychology the status of real sciences, while they are clearly pseudo-sciences. They follow the forms, they go through the rituals, gather data etc.. but it 's just a mockery, kind of a "science cargo cult". I guess prof. Starbird has more of a pure mathematics than scientific culture, and just wanted to use interesting applications of statistics about human life, but still it s dangerous and harmful to convey the idea that social science and psychology deserve the same level of trust and credibility than science.

history.title: The Man Who Never Was
history.review_title: Lesser known, (should be better known) but excellent WWII film!
history.text: I can't convey in a short review how much I love this movie! It's one of my all time favorite WWII films, along with No Man is an Island and Heaven Knows Mr. Allison. This movie, based on the true story of British Operation Mincemeat, hooks you right from the beginning. It has it all--a great story, suspense, a great script, great direction, likable characters, everything. One of my favorite scenes is where they are dressing the body getting ready to put it into the shipping canister and bombs are falling onto the streets above them and they just keep right on working as if everything is normal. The whole angle with the Nazi spy in London, hunting down info on Major Martin is suspenseful and makes this film into a genuine spy thriller as well. The ending is incredible. Josephine Griffin is wonderful as Webb's steadfast assistant, Pam and so is Gloria Grahame as the lovelorn Lucy. The film, having been made in the 1950's, still has that 1940's look to it and as such, it transports you to wartime London. Nothing inappropriate, just good clean, suspenseful entertainment. For the price, this film is a must own. If only they made more like this one. Martin genuine, indeed!

history.title: I Confess (DVD)
history.text: I Confess is one of my favorite films and my favorite Hitchcock film. This film was beautifully shot in Quebec. I prefer films in color but in this case, within the city landscape, the black and white is perfect with its light and shadows. Other reviewers have explained the plot--a priest hears a confession from a murderer and then, slowly, circumstantial evidence begins to point to him and yet, he can't say anything at all to defend himself because of the seal of confession. Montgomery Clift is excellent as the agonized priest. His performance of this very sympathetic character is incredible. He really does convey so much emotion with his eyes. Someone should have written a song called "Montgomery Clift Eyes"! (Although that doesn't have quite the same ring as "Bette Davis Eyes"...) The dialogue is also great. I did want to clarify something that another reviewer said about there being a minor "sex scandal". (Also, the DVD cover seems to imply that there is something nefarious about him.) There is no such thing in this movie. Fr. Michael is perfectly heroic and chaste in his actions as a priest. I don't want to spoil the story for anyone by explaining further but I just want any potential buyers, especially Catholic buyers, to know about Fr. Michael's heroism. It's a beautiful thing to behold. Nothing inappropriate at all, just a classic suspense film expertly directed by Hitchcock.

history.title: Mrs. Miniver (DVD)
history.review_title: I love this classic WWII homefront film!
history.text: Oh, how much I love this William Wyler film (along with Wyler's equally good homefront WWII film, The Best Years of Our Lives) These two films are essential for any lover of classic films. What do I love so much about Mrs. Miniver? I think it's because they seem like a real family, so well do the actors capture the dynamics of family life in this human drama. Their concern for their son Vin as he enters the Air Force is palpable. There are so many classic scenes--the Minivers jumping out of bed when they hear the roar of Vin's squadron flying over their country home and the look of concern on their faces as they peer into the night sky; the look of anger and fear on Kay's face as German bombs fall into their formerly peaceful world as they huddle together in their bomb shelter in their yard; Kay's encounter with the wounded but still plenty arrogant German pilot; the look of horror on the faces of Kay and Carol as a fighter plane flies right over their car and crashes into a tree, bursting into flames right before them; the final tragedy and subsequent inspirational sermon by the pastor. I could go on and on. So many wonderful, dramatic scenes and nuances within scenes. Also, the dialogue is fantastic because it comes off as so realistic. Greer Garson is terrific as is Teresa Wright. And Christopher Severn is adorable as little Toby: "I'm going through a phase! I'm going through a phase!" If you've never seen this movie do yourself a favor and buy this dvd. It's a keeper!

history.title: The Best Years of Our Lives
history.text: This film is at the top of my list of personal favorites and is, along with Mrs. Miniver, my favorite of all William Wyler's films. If there were ever three characters that you root for it's these three guys. My favorite is Dana Andrews' character Fred. He really struggles with finding a decent job and, having had similar issues in my own life with being unskilled, I could really relate to his predicament. After fighting the war in Europe as a bombardier, helping to save civilization from tyranny, he winds up going back to the drug store where he once worked making ice cream sodas before the war. Fred also struggles with what we call PTSD today. The scenes that portray this are very moving. Then there's Homer who lost both of his hands in the war. Homer is played by Harold Russell, a real life army veteran who lost both of his hands in an accident. No need for any Forrest Gump, CGI shenanigans here. (This non-professional actor went on to win an Academy Award for his performance.) Homer's girl Wilma still loves him despite his crushing feelings of inadequacy. The scene between Homer and Wilma, played by Cathy O'Donnell, later in the film is one of the most touching scenes in any film ever made. It simply has to be seen. Finally there's Al who struggles a bit with the bottle although this is not overplayed. In fact, and I think it's what makes it so good is that the entire film avoids turning into a sentimental cliche. It is stirring but not syrupy and it stays unpredictable and maintains subtlety throughout. It's a long film but it's so good, the time just flies by.

history.title: Florence Nightingale
history.review_title: Fine TV film that shows the beauty of sacrifice!
history.text: I just got finished watching Florence Nightingale and was pleasantly surprised by this made for TV film from 1985. I thought it was well done. Are there some negatives? Sure, but there are many more positives. I know some would quibble about Jaclyn Smith's poor British accent but I got used to it and was able to overlook it because there is a lot of beauty in the film, specifically, the beauty of sacrifice. I actually thought Smith did a fine acting job otherwise. Though I suspect that they have taken considerable license with her life story it still made for a good film which conveyed well the sacrifice that she made. It would have been so easy to remain comfortable in England, a well-to-do lady with a husband and a stately home of her own, but Florence's calling was for others. She fully believed she was called by God to help the sick. Whether she had to battle such temptation toward the married life I don't know but it sure made for stirring drama. It would be interesting to see a modern film made about her life. It's too bad that they can't make more films about heroes and heroines like Florence. They probably feel that they wouldn't make enough money from films like that, so they stick with making 57 Spider Man movies instead. I guess those of us who long for films about true heroes and not superheroes will have to make do with TV movies from the 80's. Of course, if they did make a modern film about her they would probably put a nude scene in it and riddle it with F bombs. Anyway, for the price this is a worthwhile film.

history.title: Johnny Belinda
history.text: This is a really fantastic film, one of the best from this era. I'm not really interested in seeing violence against women in films and while, any rape is of course a vicious act, I was concerned about how it was depicted. (There's too much violence against women in films today, not to mention in the porn industry, which preys upon the sinful male desire to dominate women.) I wanted to be able to watch it with my daughter to introduce the subject without traumatizing her. So, I finally decided to take a chance and I'm glad I did. The scene in question is only a very small part of the film and it quickly fades to black. No worries. The rest of it is just a wonderful story of overcoming adversity which has been well reviewed by several others. I love it because it is heartwarming without being too sappy. history.title: A Man for All Seasons (Special Edition)
history.review_title: Transports you back in time to the 16th century!
history.text: This is one of my favorite films ever. I watch it just about once a year. From the very beginning, as strident chords resound while the camera alternately glimpses the English countryside and follows the King's courtier in a row boat up the Thames on his way to summon Thomas More to court, we are transported back in time to the 16th century. Great music, direction, pacing, acting, dialogue, everything. The film has a beauty about it that I wish I'd see in more films. Fred Zinnemann's use of shots of surrounding landscapes at various intervals throughout the film should be studied by all students of film. Witness a man who refused to compromise his convictions and paid the ultimate price. More was one of only a handful of influential people in England who had the courage to refuse to go along with Henry VIII's shenanigans. We know what human beings are capable of regarding evil. More's action is a testament to what human beings are capable of moving in the opposite direction--sacrifice for a cause that is dear to one's heart and soul, in this case the cause being the sanctity of the marriage vow. My favorite quote from the film: "When statesmen forsake their own private conscience for the sake of their public duties, they lead their country by a short route to chaos."

history.review_title: Your Politically Correct Guide to the Crusades
history.text: I'm starting to lose patience with these fantasy movies masquerading as 'historical'. hat we have here is Orlando Bloom - who is not only the skinniest blacksmith I ever saw, especially by medieval standards, but also possesses the sensibilities and attitudes of a late 20th century college student - travels from a stunningly snowy France (?) to Palestine to atone for his sins. Not only does he turn out to be a better fighter than all the Knights who've been doing this for years or decades, as well as a brilliant strategerist and rousing, inspiring orator (he's a blacksmith, remember?), no, somewhere along the way my homeboy O also seems to have developed superpowers, which becomes evident when he repeatedly bare-knuckle punches someone in the full-face helmet......without turning his hand into mush. He also gets the girl (duh, he's Orlando....), the female audience get their 50 Shades of Older Woman/Young Hawt Guy, the Knights Templar are all Evil, the Saracens are Noble...oh, you knew that already? The priest is, naturally, a craven coward, the King's speech miraculously unaffected by his severe leprosy-caused deformity, the taking of Saladin's sister, which historically did not happen, does happen here (Templars...Evil...you know...) and on and on. Mr. Bloom does seem to have paid attention during his time in Middle-Earth (or the director has watched his Extended Edition DVD set of Lord of the Rings even more often than I have), because many of the battle scenes will not only remind you of Peter Jackson's opus, they look so very, very much the same that you almost feel transported into another movieverse entirely when the Rohirrim, I mean Knights charge, or the Orcs, no, wait a minute, those aren't Orcs...Southrons, maybe? No Oliphaunts, sorry, but they do have siege towers. No Grond, but exploding fireballs. In the 12th century.

history.title: Day of the Siege
history.text: Often have actual historical events been as distorted as they are in this movie. The Ottoman Turkish siege of Vienna in the summer of 1683 lasted about 2 months, with deprivations and heroics on the part of the defenders - outnumbered 20:1 - on an almost unbelievable scale, Do we get a sense of that? No. Do we get to know the citizens of Vienna or Ernst Rüdiger Graf Starhemberg, who, despite being grievously wounded early on, commanded the defense of his city? No. Do we learn about the horrific atrocities committed by the invaders on the population of the Balkans on their way to Vienna or the population of the areas surrounding Vienna before and during the siege? No. Do we get the bloody drama of sappers digging tunnels - the Turks in order to blow up the walls, the Viennese in order to stop them - and the desperate hand-to-hand combat ensuing inside those tunnels? No. Do we get the many assaults on the walls, led by Janissaries - European children kidnapped from their homes, raised as Muslims in Turkey and taught to be soldiers of the Sultan - repulsed time and again by a small number of fiercely determined defenders? No. Do we get the frustrating, time-consuming political haggling behind the scenes, attempts to alert a sleeping Europe to the deadly threat appearing yet again on its' southeastern frontier? No. What we do get is a fantasy story about an Italian monk (What? Oh wait, it's an Italian-Polish co-production, Italian director, probably mostly paid by RTI, that's why) with near-supernatural powers and a weirdly concocted love story between his best Muslim friend (???) and a blonde (!!!) Turkish girl. And we get the always gorgeous Isabella Orsini having a bad dream, which may be the best part of the movie. So, if you like fantasy movies, this one's ok, but they forgot the wizards and dragons. If you like costume dramas, it'll do. If you want actual history, you're much better off with books.
