history.review_title: Are you down with the League? The film has serious problems
history.text: My review of "Justice League" for the end of 2017: With my two days off I had taken a first look at the Christmas time holiday films, including (at least for me) the highly anticipated DC expansion movie spectacular sequal to Batman Vs Superman, Warner Brothers 2017 "Justice League". This past summer's "Wonder Woman" was a very surprising smash hit and worthy as a member of the "Batman" DC unvirse, but last year's "Suicide Squad" was not so great. Well from what I heard online, and from the noise made by critics Warner Brothers had decided to tone down the darker hard elemental tones and simply just produce a lighter more kid-teen friendly film. DC & Warner Bros were upset about the reaction to the hard lined darker B vs S, & I felt made the wrong decision by making this film lighter instead of what I believed worked perfectly before. This move might have been taken in positively by most comic book movie fans out there (in fact many fans posted happy reviews online via Youtube), but not by me because I really generally only enjoy harder more R rated themed material only rarely on occassion taking the time to see a G or PG movie. One of the reasons I had loved the 2008 - 2012 Christopher Nolan-Bale- Michael Caine trilogy along with waaaay back 1989's Michael Keaton version honestly because they were tougher, more edgy dark adult themed movies. Thus unlike EVERYONE else on planet Earth, maybe lets say ten other human beings who saw the film, I was one of the very few who really enjoyed the Hell out of 2016's "Batman Vs Superman" minus the Doomsday character scene. So yes this movie is lighter, but that does not mean it is not enjoyable because at the end of the day it is still a decent film (but could have been much better). Quick synopsis, a few years after the events of "B Vs S" about half the Earth's population morns Superman. Batman-Bruce Wayne played again by Ben Affleck, has been waiting for the time when his theory of creepy alien invaders will attack Earth. One night in a roof top fist fight with an ugly street thug city robber, his theory is proven correct and he has to get his plan into gear of searching, finding, meeting, and bringing together the world's superheros into one team. We learn that Wonder Woman lives her new life as an art restorer on the other side of the Atlantic ocean in England or France, (across from Bruce Wayne who still fights crooks in Gotham IE we assume Jersey City-New York). When, what I guess are, a crew of well dressed gunmen bank robber-Terrorists attack London, she is called into action as her true superhero self. (If these dudes are bombers then why go to the trouble of robbing the bank with AR-15s? But I guess that does not matter). One thing that I found a bit frustrating, & maybe this was done on purpose, but we still do not know who Wonder Woman romantically will get involved with. We had slight hints that maybe she does find Batman-Bruce Wayne attractive (but they also have heated arguments), but we then noticed scenes where she was very attracted to Superman, and even our new hero Arthur Curry the Atlantian Marine named Aquaman has his own crush on her plus vice versa. Well Gal Godet's character has three masculine handsome studs to pick from. I wanted to see something more than what was given to us. So thus the plot comes together & the team forms to save Earth. The special effects work very well, action stunt sequences are pretty first rate, but the film does have some problems namely, at least in my humble opinion, a very lame and weak villain (ugly blueish very tall guy with an axe & falcon helmut). I felt this villain's origins were weak, cheesy, too cartoonish, & I never once understood how he & his insect like shock troops traveled appearing out of the sky from no where as if he had a cosmic time warp key or a wormhole device. The Cosmic Cube, or the All Spark, box things were also a complete copy of "Transformers" and did not move the plot convincely enough. Nothing is technically explained well enough in regards to this villain nor his technology, & his rationale was not very moving nor intersting. His insect alien soldiers were very video game like, easily shot with a space rifle or punched in the face a few times where they splatter into green goo. At the end I do think Nolan's trilogy (2007-2012), Tim Burton's first 1989 movie, B Vs S of 2016, & this past summer's "Wonder Woman" are much better films, the movie is still watchable. I also personally did not care for in the least the "Flash" character, he is the comic relief & he is popular with fans but he was just not cool enough to be on the equal stage with my boy Batman-Bruce Wayne, or my new homegirl Wonder Woman. He in my view really sucked and brought the film down, but not as much as the loser villain had. These parts of the film could have been written better, but over all the effects are great, the costumes are pretty darn fantastic, the artistic imagery is in the golden age of comic books, and the action sequences do play out nicely enough for me to give this movie a solid C with neither thumbs up nor thumbs down, only yet another so so movie that could have been a thousand times better.

Nicholas Jarecki for Arbitrage. Should his name ever come to my attention again I will avoid the product related to him. All my life I've studied writing, editing, entertaining in creative forms as a matter of a love for it. Stephen King, very well loved, doesn't cross my desk after years of horrible "non" endings. I'm inclined to writers like Dean Koontz and J. Michael Straczynski... people who appreciate their audiences and don't play idiocy with them. They have the guts to write a climax that leads to a sensible conclusion that satisfies the consumer. If you think "Highly praised" aka "art" or "artistic" is "just wonderful", then waste your life watching movies like this one. Better still, find a foreign film where you can read the closed captions and miss the acting for your entertainment... personally, I would prefer a book if I have to read. You have to take this review based on its title, Instant Review... I rarely get upset unless my valuable time is infringed upon. If you don't mind being moderately entertained for around 100 minutes and then going to the bathroom and missing the whole climax and conclusion, you'll like this film. I can't give zero stars, one star would insult the 95 or so minutes of great acting and tension you'd expect from 'drama'. So two stars with the warning, 100 minutes are YOUR minutes and you deserve to enjoy all of those minute, not 95% of them.

history.review_title: I'm sorry. I'm too old for this. And I think.
history.text: I suppose this is for people who liked Blair witch project, which I hated, and every one in that first person video blog genre. It was unbearable after 12 minutes, but being determined I waited until they throw balls at each other's faces that had a little meaning. A commercial alerted me it was time to pour salt in my eyes, and fill out government forms.

history.review_title: You can enjoy this movie if you try. I still don't like the meaning of "apologetics"
history.text: I saw that a friend mentioned he watched this movie in a facebook post and that he liked it. That sparked my interest so I looked if it was on Amazon Prime. Hooray for me! I would put it on my wishlist and maybe watch it someday. But then started reading the reviews. That convinced me to stay up all night and watch it. The top 5 “most helpful” reviews were 4 one star, and 1 two star reviews. It was hated by everyone pretty uniformly. Now having watched it, I understand the bad reviews. There were more good than bad reviews according to their little line graph but Amazon only showed me the horrible reviews to read. God knows why... (pun intended) I'm giving 3 stars. That might be high looking at it one way, might be low looking at it differently. The movie is almost pure cliché and is predictable. Many of the characters more shallow than 10 cent detective novel characters from the 30s. One spot I particularly disliked was a violent scene covered with very loud annoying music where the lyrics were clearly saying what the director wanted the viewer to think about the scene the music was destroying. Bad taste. In my opinion the movie mistakenly and poorly portrays Christians. I think only Josh, the primary “apologetics” freshman student, escapes being horribly displayed as “Christian”. Atheists and anti-theists get the same unfair treatment, being portrayed poorly or mistakenly. I was able to enjoy the movie. I can overlook a lot of producer and director idiocy and still enjoy a story. The one part I did enjoy was the Christian apologetics. I'll never get used to the meaning of that word, “apologetics” as explaining in favor of something. Seems to me, if someone is for something or believes in something, explaining their favorable leanings is not apologetic in any way. But we have the language we have, so there it is. There is some drama and tension there, but it is unintentionally shallow. There are characters you can hate and some you can like, so it is possible to enjoy this movie. If you decide to give it a go, just go in knowing it is a very bad portrayal of Christians meaning to be favorable of Christians, sadly attempting to portray “anti-Christians” poorly and in unlikely ways. Don't misunderstand, I'm Christian and want you to 'be saved' and love my God as much as I do, but I would rather poor salt into my eyes than do this movie to you as an effort to convince you my spiritual inclinations should be your spiritual inclinations. I think what the movie tries to do, cause and effect in people, it produces the opposite effect.

history.review_title: Turing test on steroids. A mystery. Is it, or is it not?
history.text: I'm going with 3 stars, but understand... it could be 2 stars or up to 5 stars. This one will hit people differently. I don't know “who to”, or “how to” recommend this movie. I'm certain some folks will say, “brilliant”, while others will say, “take a nap, your dream will be more entertaining.” I usually write the review right after seeing the movie. I didn't on this one, and now, after it has soaked in a bit I'm a little stuck on what to think. Some people would call that a plus because “It made me think”. I'll give them that. I don't mean to be petty, but to watch this one I judged it entirely by it's cover. Sure, I love good science fiction but if I'm honest, the sex appeal of the movie poster sold the movie. Sorry to be so pathetic on that account. Once started though I was hooked. I'm glad they didn't play around with “the start”. This one, whoosh, you're in the story. The movie is a play on the Turing Test (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_test). I think this is infinitely interesting to science fiction affectionados. So “interesting topic” gets kudos. There is a minimum of characters which leaves writers room to really twist the suspense. Call this another plus. Writers and directors famously give their characters conflicting goals, put them together and see what happens. There is definitely some of that going on in this movie. It seemed much more of a mystery than science fiction to me, although some kudos do go to the special effects department. I recall being in “the guessing mode” most of the time. Several guesses I hit, right on, several I missed entirely. So it does pull off “mystery”. What to think or feel about it... I'm afraid it may be quite some time before I decide either of those issues. Add a plus to “social commentary” or “intrigue”. People interested in the topic of artificial intelligence, i.e., The Turing Test, should definitely give this a watch. I think mystery addicts would like it more than Sci-fi/Action Adventure/Space/ folks. Ultimately I think we all love a good mystery.

history.title: Gone Girl
history.text: If you want DRAMA with a healthy dose of mystery, you'll be entertained. Four stars would be an honest entertainment value rating by my estimate. I thought it was ok (3 stars.) My feelings about it hover in the 1-2 star range. Great acting that pulled off the movie wonderfully. Make-up and Rosamund Pike are almost certain award winners. It has nothing to do with his acting but I'm not terribly fond of Ben Affleck, and I was oblivious of anyone else in this movie. I don't recall any prompting to watch “Gone Girl” but somewhere along the line I became impressed that I should watch this movie, even before Jupiter Rising which would normally appeal to me much more. Now let me go sideways for a moment. It may be a spoiler so move along at this point with my recommendation that this is a DRAMA on steroids. Now sideways, and spoiler... Glenn Close is an brilliant actress, attractive, and NOT in this movie. I mention her because I have had an irrational but reflexive dislike of Glenn Close since watching Fatal Attraction in 1987. This movie had me cringing almost as much as Fatal Attraction. This movie isn't a Fatal Attraction plot clone, but it certainly gave me the same feelings that Fatal Attraction did. I could have dreamed up a dozen endings I may have liked better... well, it is what it is, and my “woulda, coulda, shoulda” is irrelevant.

history.review_title: It looked delicious. Hope it isn't DOA.
history.text: Entertainment of this kind is just pitiful these days. A person could go crazy the way shows are selected, continued, picked up, or cancelled. So what if I liked it? Lots of great reviews, probably be costly to the consumer if they pick it up...and I don't think they should have made a pilot unless they had a lot of certainty about offering it. A broadcaster that made solid 2-3-4 year commitments to new shows would win my loyalty way over what is going on these days. I'm leaning towards a policy of ignoring all new offerings, making note of the ones I think may be interesting. Waiting 3 years and if they are not cancelled in the middle of a scene..., test the water and actually jump in if it is truly interesting. I was suckered into watching this. Thought it was already picked up and well on its way on Amazon. Having dipped in for a taste, I'll be marking this one down as something to look forward to in a few years. It looked delicious.

history.review_title: Tried and True on Two Fronts
history.text: This idea, contrary to some opinions is an old one. This one is exactly John Scalzi’s, “Old Man’s War”… series idea but Ol’ John Perry had no idea what he was in for. In this outing of the idea Damien Hale did know… at least as much as the crippled Jake Sully in Avatar knew. Figure the dates..., and Avatar was probably “influenced” by Old Man’s War. But it is a great idea, and folks can do a lot with it. This one is a tried and true “character quest plot” which explaining creeps into the spoiler category if you don’t already know what it is. If you do, you know those are usually great stories. To me it was predictable. Not the movie's fault that… I’ve read a lot. The plot has a couple ways to go. The way this one went is probably the most popular and well liked. I was a little surprised it wasn’t “more”. I think I just was not feeling the crash, bang, boom going on. I would have liked a little more getting in touch with the “past training”. I think that would have sold me on the crash, bang, boom more convincingly. Don’t misunderstand, it is a good movie. Ben Kingsley can do no wrong by me. Ryan Reynolds is working on getting there himself, and I have a spot in my heart for Natalie Martinez from the Under the Dome days. Sprinkle in some Victor Garber and you have a set of actors almost always worth watching. I enjoyed a couple of surprising plot point twists that I didn’t see coming. Movie might be worth watching for those alone. It is great when a story surprises and that isn’t an easy thing to sell to well conditioned entertainment consumers. To me this is a solid 4 stars. First review, from elsewhere, I looked at before watching the movie had me feeling like I was out in the desert looking into the night sky there were so many stars. It’s worth watching. Then you decide.

history.review_title: I liked the show. My recommendation is not so hot.
history.text: The four star rating could as easily been 5 stars. I wasn't really into the whole thing, The idea and premise didn't appeal to me, but when I sat down to binge on it anyway and I was drawn into the story. I've seen horrible reviews and ranting reviews. Mine is simple, it is entertaining and I liked it, I would have watched the 3rd season. As a recommendation I would not spend a dime on it or give it 30 seconds of your time. Syfy cancelled it abruptly. It is clear the writers and producers believed there would be a 3rd season. If you understand what that means and you want to take the ride and don't care about the destination, this could still be fun for you.

history.review_title: You'll get frustrated, bored, but hopefully the last third will make it worth your time.
history.text: I remember stopping at one hour and 12 minutes. I reviewed the movie in my mind and figured they could have cut 42 of those minutes, and probably should have. The last 40-45 minutes of the movie is worth the emotional response, and all the better if you're Christian. Make no mistake, this is a "Christian" movie, plenty of prayer and the kinds of things you'll hear from many good church folks. I understand the one star reviews, it was tedious. It could be edited to 60 or 70 minutes and come out with a more powerful movie, but I'm not the one doing to work, so if you want to get what you hoped for, you'll have to get through the first hour and twelve minutes... shortly after that I was enjoying the movie. What saddens me, is I understand writing, drama, entertainment. And as you can see from the reviews, much of the audience is not going to forgive the level of tedious boredom and inability to care for your damaged protagonist that goes on so long. That's what sticks with them. A much more stronger emotional response to the early lack of entertainment than the last 30-40 minutes that provoked a strong enough emotional response to forgive the tedious beginning for me.

history.review_title: Great Fun, A trailer to a new cancelled series never aired? Who's idea was that?
history.text: Last two years I've watched Amazon go from a top company to a company I can barely stand. Who's idea is it to have half a dozen new shows, market them like crazy and offer ONE episode where obviously there is a season of episodes? I loved this concept or idea, but it is like a trailer for a cancelled show that never started. I hope someone is paying attention to reviews at Amazon and that someone will fire whoever started running this company into the ground the last couple years. I think I'll skip renewing my prime membership. They've added a lot of totally worthless nonsense like this to present the illusion of value.

history.title: Challenge of the Gladiator
history.review_title: Good quality transfer but not 2.35 ratio
history.text: A surprisingly good transfer. It's taken from an American International TV print and is slightly letterboxed (1.77). The image is mostly sharp and the color is very good. This DVD is far better in quality than most of the other Sword and Sandal films released here. The movie itself is a mishmash of history which involves Spartacus and Nero (huh?). Rock Stevens (aka Peter Lupus) makes for a likable and handsome hero. Also on hand are those two villainous genre regulars Massimo Serato and Livio Lorenzon. If you are a fan of Sword and Sandal films I recommend this DVD.

history.title: Never Say Goodbye
history.text: An outstanding widescreen and color transfer from the Universal Vault Series. The movie itself is great too. Rock Hudson gives a terrific performance and the unjustly forgotten Cornell Borchers is both beautiful and affecting. A wonderful movie in every respect.

history.title: Risen
history.text: Unfortunately, not enough people here have reviewed the movie and far too many have used this venue as a religious forum. No one has mentioned that this is the third film version of the story. In 1986 Keith Carradine and Harvey Keitel starred in the first version which was titled The Inquiry. In 2007 a second version, The Final Inquiry, was released starring Daniele Liotti and Dolph Ludgren. Both are fine films and in many ways superior to Risen. Risen is a good movie but not a great one. It is by far the most religious of the three films and at times seemed very preachy. Nevertheless, it is nice to see a decent Biblical film in the wake of the dreadful Noah and Exodus: Gods and Kings.

history.title: Spartacus - Der Titan mit der eisernen Faust - un
history.text: This German DVD is a beautiful, remastered transfer of Hero of Rome starring Gordon Scott. It's really only a three star worthy entry in the Sword and Sandal genre but the stunning widescreen color presentation merits another star. It has an English language soundtrack option too! You won't find a better copy of this film anywhere.

history.title: Prince Of Players
history.text: Another wonderful early Fox widescreen movie gets a pan and scan presentation. Who the hell makes these decisions at Fox Cinema Archives? They must be total idiots. And to add insult to injury the box art prominently features the word CinemaScope. Another favorite movie I'll skip buying thanks to a shoddy Fox DVD presentation.

history.title: Ator the Iron Warrior ( Ator il guerriero di ferro ) ( Iron Warrior ) [ NON-USA FORMAT, PAL, Reg.0 Import - Italy ]
history.text: This is without a doubt one of the worst films I have ever seen in all my years of movie watching. There is nothing redeemable about it in any way. Director Alfonso Brecia (herein billed as Al Bradley) actually made some decent movies back in the heyday of the Sword and Sandal films. But apparently by the time he made Ator the Iron Warrior, Alfonso had forgotten everything he ever knew about filmmaking. And the production values are nil. Some of the scenes are actually shot on leftover sets from the movie Popeye; not the most logical choice for a Sword and Sorcery movie to say the least. The two leads, Miles O'Keefe and Savina Gersak, are saddled with terrible hairdos in addition to having no screen presence whatsoever. This Italian DVD has an English language option but the sound quality varies from scene to scene. The image is sharp and does have nice color as if that could possibly compensate for how rotten the movie is.

history.title: SODOMA Y GOMORRA
history.text: Poor quality, Spanish language only DVD of Sodom and Gomorrah. The transfer looks worse than a VHS tape...far worse. The Fox Cinema Archives release of this movie, while not letterboxed, is still the best version out there.

history.title: Pegasus Vs. Chimera
history.text: I can't believe all the positive reviews for this turkey. It's really, really bad. Vesuvius Productions are giving Asylum competition in the "awful movies for TV" market. No production values, awful costumes, unappealing and poor actors, lousy CGI effects. What more could you ask for? It's not even "funny bad." It's just BAD.

history.title: Revolt of the Praetorians
history.text: Not the best Sword and Sandal movie by a long shot but it is good to have an English language DVD (DVD-R actually) of it with a decent widescreen transfer and good color. This is the longer European version and some of the scenes are in Italian because they were never dubbed into English. One of these scenes has English subtitles but the others do not. No big deal as it is primarily action stuff anyway. Richard Harrison never looked better and Moira Orfei's color coordinated wigs are a real hoot. If you are a fan of the genre this is certainly worth the price. The one downside to this DVD is the very abrupt ending.

history.title: One Million B.C.
history.review_title: Beautiful Transfer of a Classic Film
history.text: UCLA Film Archives did a great job restoring this film. There isn't a blemish to be seen and the image is very sharp. Certainly this is the best the movie has looked since it came out in 1940. I was surprised at how closely the famous Hammer Films remake followed the original, until the last 15 minutes or so. One Million B.C. is an underrated classic. Hopefully this new VCI release will garner it the respect it deserves.

targets.title: Walking With Dinosaurs (Blu-ray 3D / DVD Combo Pack)

history.text: Strange movie. Billed as a romantic comedy, and I guess it started out that way, but it devolved into a VERY religious drama with a very sad (if true-to-life) ending. Not at all a feel-good movie. I wanted something light and funny and was left feeling sad. I'm a devout Christian and enjoy some of the overtly Christian movies out there like War Room, for example, but this wasn't just generic Christian theology, it was LDS doctrine, straight up, no ice. I was disappointed.

history.review_title: Tender Love Story of Two Soul Mates
history.text: This is a tender and touching story of two people, one with Down's Syndrome, who fall in love and see beyond the obvious to the beauty of each other's souls. They connect on the soul level and find a beautiful relationship there. I honestly have never met a couple like this, and so I'm left with the feeling it is too good to be true--it strikes me as not overly believable. I WISH our world were this accepting. The dialog is sometimes stilted, and as others have mentioned the movie seems to be a low-budget production, but the message is inspiring, if not completely credible.

Some humorous portions but overall uninspiring. I wouldn't bother watching it again. I usually like the old movies, but this isn't one of them. The ending was a bit unexpected, and that was a novel twist, but nothing so riveting as to make me watch it again.

history.title: One Christmas Eve
history.text: I've been watching this movie for "forever," so when Amazon offered it for $6.99 (or thereabouts) instead of the Hallmark price of $20+/-, I was thrilled. I was so excited to watch it. But it was a serious disappointment. The puppy was adorable. The characters that were thrown together for this Christmas Eve were interesting but not terribly believable. And the string of crises they encountered were over the top--who slipped and fell on a kid's sled and broke an ankle; who broke an arm falling through a hole in a construction site; who got robbed at gunpoint; whose vehicle first died, and then fell through an ice-covered pond to its demise; who narrowly escaped a fire (caused by a puppy); who suffered the effects of smoke inhalation.... I could go on and on, but I won't. A crisis or two keeps one on the edge of her seat, but sitting on the edge for too long, gives one a butt ache! The ending where the whole gang exchanges gifts of the heart and has a communal meal together is nice, but not nice enough to make me watch the whole thing over again. Wearying.

history.title: Priceless (DVD)
history.review_title: R.E.L.I.G.I.O.U.S. Movie with a Potent Message
history.text: Despite the many one-star reviews, I enjoyed the movie. I DO think Amazon could do better in labeling religious movies as such. All the deceptive advertising accomplishes is to anger those who'd rather not be surprised to find a movie is religiously "biased." Knowing a bit about the Smallbones' stories helped me appreciate the movie more; these guys really live and believe in the message they're trying to get out there. No, it's probably not the best-made movie you've ever seen, but it has a powerful message--as Dale tells James once, "You can't go back, once you begin on this mission." To me the obvious message is for everyone to get involved and stop human trafficking. And I loved the positive ending of the movie.

history.review_title: Heartwarming Movie About Two War Heroes
history.text: Difficult rating this between a four and a five. I really enjoyed the movie, despite the inaccuracies of military protocol, etc., and mis-portrayal of Megan as a troubled young woman escaping her family. (If you're interested in the facts vs. the Hollywood story, you can read it here: www dot historyvshollywood dot com slash reelfaces slash megan-leavey slash.) The beauty of the Hollywood version of the story, which is certainly true of many military dogs and their handlers, is that both the dog and his handler grew to be more than they could have been without each other. It's a beautiful story that highlights the sacrifices men and women and dogs make in serving in our military. Well worth the watch, I think.

As another reviewer said, the message was powerful, but the movie was not. The lead character was not at all believable in his role, and the conversations between him and his family members were wooden, at best. I guess what bothered me most was there was no true emotion--no pure joy, no raw anger, no hatred, nothing. I'm sorry, as the story line drew me in initially. It could have been a great movie. (I dozed off several times about 2/3 of the way through, and when I woke up, I was able to pick up the story, just as if I'd been sitting on the edge of my seat watching the whole time.)

history.title: A Christmas Tree Miracle
history.review_title: Touching Story with a Great Message
history.text: Read all the negative reviews and wasn't sure I'd like the movie, but I thoroughly enjoyed it. The acting was a little stilted, and the characters a little wooden at times, but the message was well worth absorbing--family and love and kindness are worth a great deal more than monetary riches.

history.title: Sacred Vow
history.text: I was looking forward to watching this video; the plot seemed like a good one, and it was supposedly based on a true story, but the ending left me feeling cheated somehow--not that life couldn't have turned out this way, but I felt a bit like someone was toying with my emotions. I won't watch it again. The theme of love conquering all (and of forgiveness winning out over all obstacles) was a worthwhile one. But the way the wife handled the ending was disturbing to me.

Definitely a girly movie; lots of emotion runs through it, and I love Christopher Gorham--he's so believably genuine. I didn't catch on to the flashback/dream sequence throughout until the ending. Totally surprised me at the end. Enjoyed it. You may, too.

history.title: How to Get Away with Murder: Season 2
history.text: Very dark and a low sense of morality in every character. Spoiler: Even the best succumbs in the second season. If they'd all do the right thing they would save themselves a lot of personal agony. But this is the way the writers want to go these days, even Disney. Poor Walt - it would be hell for him to see where some of his company productions are going. Viola Davis is excellent in this, but I would have liked to see her work with the student lawyers on cases without all the personal drama. You can't trust the Disney name any more. Our country needs hope, not this depressing stuff. I threw this away. I wouldn't pass this on to anybody else. 'Why don't sharks eat lawyers? Professional courtesy."

history.title: Monster Hunt English Language Version
history.text: weird story but very good 3D.

history.title: Road to Rio
history.text: very slow going for us 21st century folks. Story is episodic and just plain silly. I think Bob was funniest when he worked on his own with an audience in his TV specials. Blu-ray upgrades these movies for fans who remember the 'road pictures'.

history.title: Doctor Blake Mysteries: Season Three (DVD)
history.review_title: Excellent murder mystery series with many twists and turns - a must buy for mystery fans
history.text: This series has really hooked me. Craig McIachlan is wonderful in the role of a doctor whose father (also a doctor) was dearly loved but whom he feels compared to constantly. The series is set in a small town in Australia in the 50's and Doctor Blake struggles not only with the horrors of his time served in the Australian army during World War II in the Pacific (which included being imprisoned in a Japanese prison camp) but also the disappearance of his wife and daughter during the war. My father-in-law also served in the Pacific in WWII, and while I know the American side of the war pretty well, I know next to nothing about the other countries that fought with us. If that is not enough, Doctor Blake is a police surgeon who follows his conscience but not always the rules. So besides being a cleverly written murder mystery series, you have the police procedural, his work in 50's medicine and forensics in Australia, and the cultural scene in Australia over 60 years ago. There are also secrets about him and other cast members that come out as the episodes unfold adding to the mystery.The supporting cast is excellent and you would not want to part with any of them. I'm so glad I took a chance on this series and have already ordered season 4.

history.title: Ghost in the Shell 2017
history.review_title: a cautionary tale with a lot to think about
history.text: This is a movie that makes you think about where we are headed and what the future will look like if we stay on the path we are on. Scarlett Johansson is excellent as Major - the Ghost in the Shell. She obviously put her heart and soul into the part (as she does in everything else I have seen her in). Fans of the manga and the anime versions may not be totally satisfied with her, but the author of the manga seemed thrilled to have her play the part (see the features). The supporting cast was excellent as well and I cannot say enough about the CG effects and holograms. Hong Kong was used for the city streets with CG enhancements so it seemed like a very real place. With the holograms, 3d is definitely the only way to go to see this movie. The story was a bit confusing for me as a first timer seeing it. I think the director assumed everyone who would be interested in the movie would already know the manga or have seen the anime. But it was not so confusing that you couldn't keep up and the confusion helped you connect to Major's experience since she was also struggling with who she was. Throughout the film, I was arguing with myself as to whether I wanted to keep it in my collection of Asian films (which is rapidly growing). But by the time it was over, I was sure this was a film that I would watch again.

history.title: Lucifer: The Complete First Season [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: The devil , but a very nice guy
history.text: This is a series which is depressing at times but it also helps to sort out our own beliefs about sin and the devil, as well as God and angels. When Lucifer rails against the silly interpretations of the devil and the fact that we blame him for our own bad behavior, it is very funny. It is also very human to blame others for mistakes we make and sins we commit and the devil is as good as any other to blame so that we don't have to take responsibility. But this series is not always a comedy - all the emotions have their part to play in the stories. Which leads me to Lucifer's therapist. I am a therapist myself and of course the code of ethics of counselors and therapists would not allow some of her behavior and she would lose her license. However, her actual work in sessions with Lucifer is very good, leading me to suspect that the writer has been to therapy or has a consultant who is a good counselor. And so I love the therapist character and I like the fact that not only Lucifer but Maze, Amenadiel and even 'mom' have to talk to her at one time or another. I also love the fact that Lucifer cannot lie and so he tells everyone he is the devil and they don't believe him. I love the soul searching Lucifer does about his relationship with his father (the actor who eventually plays the 'father' is excellent - I'd like to see him show up again) since many of us question our relationship with God and whether God loves us. The story arc about Lucifer's mother, turns out to be thought-provoking too, although I don't think we have a goddess in the religious traditions that call the devil Lucifer. This 'Mom' is manipulative, pretty self-centered and you never can tell when she is lying or not, the real-life experience of some people with their mothers. But since this is a show that takes itself fairly lightly, we flow along with 'mom' as well as Amenadiel, a character I also like - someone who does the wrong thing to get the right thing done and then regrets it for the rest of his life. For me this show is not just a quirky police procedural, but a challenge to compare the writers' ideas with my own. So now I own the first two seasons and am looking forward to where the third will go.

history.title: In This Corner Of The World (Blu-ray + DVD)
history.review_title: A history lesson from an old enemy who is now a friend
history.text: The fact that some reviewers seem surprised at the ending of this movie supports my belief that generations of Americans are not learning history any more. This is sad because history does repeat itself. Just as people went to see 'Titanic' without knowing what happened to it, it seems some viewers heard the word Hiroshima and couldn't predict the ending of this movie. I am 74. Pearl Harbor was just as big a surprise to my parents' generation as the Twin Towers in New York was to Americans in 2001. In 1941 and for a long time afterward we Americans could not get over our anger at the Japanese which was understandable - thousands died because of their attack on Pearl Harbor and the subsequent consequences. But perhaps now after more than 70 years distance we are able to understand what the Japanese went through in those dark years, and feel as bad for them as we did for ourselves. "War is hell" and this is a history lesson we still need to learn. Hating the other guy for whatever reason is a mistake whether he is next door or across the world. Building for a future where all share in the understanding that we are all human is better than dwelling in the past and continuing to hate and kill. I can't give this movie a five because I wouldn't show it to a child and cause them grief. But nevertheless, it starts a conversation not just for Americans but for others around the world. Who is an enemy? Do we have a right to kill someone if they have done nothing to harm anyone? How is it that old enemies become friends years later? What does war accomplish if anything?

history.review_title: Mildred Jeeter fell in love with a man that just happened to be White. As natural to her as her love of her country home.
history.text: Left out of this movie, (and also the previous production based on this couple), was the most poignant moment of authentic footage of Richard Loving when, after being asked by a pretty, blonde reporter why he didn't just divorce Mildred, he comes out of his usual shy character just long enough to look up directly at her and, as if insulted, emphatically declare that he will never divorce his wife. This movie was very slow, especially for someone that already knows the story. Even so, it captures the normalcy of this couple, this family, and the bond of love they shared, which was not Hollywood glamorous, just down-to-earth and real. It also makes almost tangible the seriousness and darkness of the situation in which they found themselves. Mr. and Mrs. Loving was more entertaining. The quirky uncertainty of Bernard Cohen, and his boy like enthusiasm. The creative license taken to create tension between Richard and Mildred over her friends in the city and her involvement in the Civil Rights Movement. The high speed chase when they outrun the police. Add touches of humor here and there. And of course, the chemistry and attraction between young Richard and Mildred. Mr. and Mrs. Loving failed, however, to portray them as simple country people that were deeply in love, with one another, their culture, and their homeland. It failed to capture their mutual devotion, Mildred's respect for Richard, and Richard's protectiveness of his wife that can be seen in real footage of them in the documentary. Loving succeeds where Mr. and Mrs. Loving fails.

SPOILER ALERT I am so disappointed in episode 1 of season 2. It was sorely lacking in authenticity. If I glanced away from the screen for a moment, and then glanced back, it was difficult to tell whether this was modern day or the past. I was willing to overlook modern-day expressions and attitudes in season 1 because there was something that felt somewhat authentic about the sets, the costumes, the hairstyles, the dialogue, and the attitudes portrayed. But season 2 seems to have lost that completely, to the point where it was annoying. I realize, of course, that it's Hollywood. Just as, according to Hollywood, Walnut Grove, (Little House on the Prairie), boasted the cleanest, toothiest, most beautiful dirt farmers ever, so Coal Valley evidently boasts the best-dressed, cleanest, toothiest, most beautiful coal mine towns people ever. Nothing at all like authentic historical pictures. In fact, they must have enjoyed modern day makeup artists, hair stylists, hair products, hair implements, and hair dyes. Abigail was my second favorite character, after Jack. But by the beginning of Season 2, she was looking much less like a widowed frontierswoman living in a coal mining town around the turn of the 20th century, and much more like Laurie Laughlin, the famous, glamorous (glamorized) actress. Ego. Okay,... But some of us like to watch historical shows because we enjoy the idea of a simpler more natural life. This attempt to fuse modern day aesthetics with historical accuracy does not work well. I fell in love with the character Elizabeth during the first season. Even though she was a rich heiress, she did not come across as spoiled. She was a roll up your sleeves, nose to the grindstone, jump right in kind of young woman. She seemed genuinely concerned with the welfare of her new friends and neighbors. But Season 2 made me dislike her. She was such a different person in Hamilton, just like Jack says. Not just different, but self-absorbed, snotty, privileged, demanding, and thoughtless. She acted like she was madly in love with Jack and Cole Valley, but once they got to Hamilton, she didn't treat him right. She invited Jack to dinner at her family's house and then proceeded to spend all of her time with Charles. She left Jack in the background and basically ignored him all evening. But then she runs to the train station to plant a big wet one on him before he leaves. Very manipulative. The second time they are in Hamilton together, she is better towards Jack, and finally gets honest with herself about Charles, but she's so nasty about Jack's brother Tom. Rude. It's natural to for her to defend her sister, but she's snide and cutting about it. It really did make me wonder who she really is. I suppose this is deliberate on the part of the writers, but I think it's a little overdone. It made me wonder if she's trustworthy. The heroin should be somewhat sympathetic. The protagonist should be likable. At the mine when she suddenly starts sobbing and saying that she's afraid of losing Jack, it's hard to buy. Bipolar? I think the writers should have had her and Jack in Hamilton again to show that she really could be as warm and loving toward him in Hamilton as she could be in the Valley. It was written as if she and Jack could only be good together in Coal/Hope Valley. Didn't the storyline in episode 1 go a little off track? The plot was hard to follow. Really, Miss Madison proved that Noah Stanton did know that the mine was unsafe when he lead those men inside, including his own son. A bittersweet victory, I should think. But, hey, the widows got PAID. And in short order, their money transported them to the future of clothing, cosmetics, hair care products, color and styling implements. Yay!
I'm hooked!

I have to admit that I am a "hearty." I love this show! The question is why? I often fall asleep with it on, and I have to say that I enjoy listening to it more than I do watching it. Watching it can be irritating. I would give it a full five star rating, but When Calls the Heart has really lost its authenticity. It started off taking mild Hollywood liberties, and each season only gets worse! The producers are obviously much more concern with aesthetics than with accuracy. A woman living in a 1910 coal mining turned saw milling town that wears white and pink to teach school everyday? Light colors would not have been practical for working with children, and it's not believable for that time period. The make-up is over the top, and not even well done this season. Elizabeth looks like a raccoon! The hairstyles are so modern that they would call for modern day products and styling tools. All of the women in that hard working town began to wear their hair lose in Season 2. Again, not realistic. By the way,...is there something wrong with dark hair??? And the remodel of Elizabeth's row house? Come on! I had to keep reminding myself of the time period. Also, a lot of forward thinking. Modern, yes, but that doesn't make it good, or right, let alone historically accurate. It should be annoying, maybe even offensive, like Stepford Wives or Pleasantville. No diversity. A few Black extras placed, not so subtly, in background shots. Maybe that is realistic? Probably not. Almost everyone is good, or at least has a very good reason for badness, and can be rehabilitated within a few minutes with a little sympathetic listening and a good talking to. So, why do I love it? I suppose because it has a peaceful feel. And it is an ideal. But Little House on the Prairie remains my favorite. Michael Landon and his crew kept it much more honest.

history.title: Strauss: Elektra - James Levine Metropolitan Opera Exclusive DVD
history.text: There's not much more I can add to the accolades already posted here, except to concur that Hildegard Behrens's Elektra is truly one of the most -- if not THE most -- superb opera performances ever captured on film. Behrens doesn't just sing or play Elektra well; she IS Elektra. Her level of commitment, both vocally and in her acting, is astounding. Happily, the rest of the cast rises to her level, particularly Deborah Voight, not the best singing actress on the planet. Here, however, she is a more than worthy partner for Behrens, if not quite her equal. Brigitte Fassbaender's Clytemnestra is indeed over the top, sometimes distractingly so, but it's fascinating to see her play to the house while Behrens plays to the camera. The juxtaposition in performance styles -- the old giving way to the new -- is one more reason this is such an important contribution to opera on film. Kudos also to Otto Schenk for the atmospheric production and rock solid direction. An essential DVD for any collection.

history.title: Jersey Boys (DVD)
history.text: First off, I have to admit to not being a huge fan of the Broadway show. I didn't care then about Frankie Valli's life and I still don't now. What the show had going for it, though, was tremendous energy and a glitzy, somewhat cheesy charm. And the music, of course. What makes the film version such a letdown is its literalness. Director Clint Eastwood has taken a Broadway musical and turned it into a rather dreary biopic with the occasional song. The film should soar as soon as the singing starts, but it just sits there. What the material needed was a Rob Marshall or Martin Scorsese, someone who knows how to energize an audience and whip up some excitement with a distinct visual style. This film has no style whatsoever, no point of view. Eastwood turned on the camera and let the actors do what they do. Okay, there's a little bit more to it than that, but it's a pretty dull affair. John Lloyd Young is, unfortunately, a large part of the problem. On stage he was electric, but here he's a cipher. The other three Seasons are much better, particularly Vincent Piazza, who's like a lightning bolt among fireflies. All in all, the film is a perfectly acceptable waste of two + hours, but it could have been a major event in the hands of a different director.

history.title: Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg [Blu-ray]
history.text: The idea of having the characters of Wagner's "Die Meistersinger von Nurnberg" Lilliputian-sized, cavorting across Hans Sach's desktop and amongst his furnishings (as if creatures out of his imagination), is a cute one; although what "cute" has to do with this particular opera is beyond me. It's a fairly benign, inoffensive conceit (as Euro-trashy conceits go), until the Grimm's fairytale creatures appear and proceed to have anal intercourse with one another (I kid you not), turning the end of Act II into a nightmarish bacchanalia. That's when I grabbed the remote, shut the thing off and walked away. Seriously, why bother at that point? I'm not averse to high concept (Chereau's Ring, Girard's recent "Parsifal"), and I'm sure that director Stefan Herheim has justifications for his interpretation, but this one is so distracting as to be comical. Too bad, as the cast, particularly the Sachs of Michael Volle, is first rate. Call me a boring traditionalist, but I would much rather watch a respectful production, like David McVicar's rapturous Glyndebourne version, than a non-sensical mess like this.

history.title: Donizetti: L'elisir d'amore [Blu-ray]
history.text: Some of director/star Rolando Villazon's ideas for his reimagined "L'Elisir d'Amore" work quite nicely. The problem is how many there are. As another reviewer said, there's a lot going on onstage at all times, which makes it very hard for the audience to focus on what's important. A director's job is to not only direct the actors, but the audience as well. Where should we look, to what singer should we be paying attention, who's story is this? These concepts pretty much go out the window when the whole stage is a three-ring circus. The very conceit of the show is one idea too many. Not content to set this "Elixir" in the American West (an idea that I can see working), Villazon gives us a film being shot about the American West in the American West, with Adina the star and the film actor playing Dulcamara also directing. The "joke" is that Nemorino, a groupie of Adina's, can't distinguish between what's happening in reality and what's part of the film. He's constantly jumping into frame, trying to save the day, frustrating the director and Adina alike. This makes the character an even greater idiot than he's usually played (and as usually interpreted by Villazon). Adding insult to injury is that this Mexican director dresses Nemorino as the stereotypical dumb Mexican peasant, complete with poncho, Cantinflas mustache and "What's going on?" expression. And where again are we supposed to be? In the accompanying documentary, Villazon references Spaghetti Westerns, so shouldn't we be in Italy? But no, the script the actors use has an English title, as are the film within the opera's title cards. And in what era exactly? We're told that the time is the 1950s, but the film being shot is a...silent movie? Huh? Makes no sense whatsoever. So many conflicting ideas, adding to the general sense that Villazon has no filter whatsoever. The singers are generally fine, particularly the lovely Miah Persson, who manages to rise above the silliness around her. Ildebrando D'Arcangelo sings well, as per usual, but is a painfully unfunny Dulcamara/director. At one point Adina shoots a gun into the air to quiet the crowd around her, and of course a bird plunges from the sky. (It's just that kind of unimaginative production; you know exactly what's going to happen next...and it does.) In this case, though, the bird is a buzzard. Watching D'Arcangelo pick up the bird and wear it like a shawl, "singing" through its mouth, mugging up a storm, is excruciating. And speaking of mugging, there's Villazon himself. I've always decried the way he plays this role, but here he's on overdrive. And as good as he sounds, it's an effort now. He looks uncomfortable, and we feel that way watching him. Yesterday I saw Laurent Pelly's gorgeous Covent Garden production of this opera, and it's everything Villazon's is not: wise, clever, simple, heartwarming, focused, simple, restrained, emotionally involving, simple. And did I mention simple? Pelly has ideas, but they stand alone so they actually mean something. Villazon, to mix metaphors, throws the kitchen sink at the wall to see what sticks. And it just ends up crashing to the floor and making a lot of noise.

history.title: The Terminal (Widescreen Edition)
history.text: This is a perfectly charming film of no consequence whatsoever. Every single one of its participants has done far better work on other projects, the possible exception being John Williams, and you can listen to his score on CD. Not a complete waste of time, but not a film that is likely to last in memory or touch you in deep ways. The cinematic equivalent of Jell-O.

history.title: Ondine
history.text: Not being familiar with this ballet, I purchased the DVD on the strength of Frederick Ashton having done the choreography. Did I say "choreography?" Other than the Act 3 wedding scene and a few random moments here and there, there seems to be very little actual dancing in this piece. A lot of pantomime, gesturing and water sprites running back and forth across the stage, yes. But the kind of complex, expressive and engaging choreography one might expect from the man who created "Cinderella," "Romeo and Juliet" and "La filled mal gardée?" Not really. Heck, even "The Tales of Beatrix Potter" has more going for it than this humorless, incomprehensible mess. Everyone does the best they can with what they're given, but it's all pretty pointless and dramaturgically absurd. (What are they all doing on that ship and where are they going?) And I can't say that it's a particularly attractive production, so there's not even much to engage the eye. All told, I'm sorry for the purchase.

history.title: Wagner: Der Fliegende Holländer (The Flying Dutchman)
history.text: Did you know that Wagner's "Der fliegende Holländer" was an indictment of the Dutch East India Company's exploitation of the indigenous South African native? Well, neither did I until I saw Andreas Homoki's completely loopy, but not uninteresting 2013 staging for Opernhaus Zurich. It doesn't quite make sense -- which is putting it mildly -- but it's entertaining in an abstract, what-the-hell's-going-on? kind of way. After a while, unfortunately, you realize that the answer is, "Not much," which is not entirely Homoki's fault. A fairly early opera in Wagner's career, it doesn't have the most cohesive libretto, with all of the dramatic tension pretty much resolved by the end of Act 2. And, for that matter, we already know what Senta's answer to the Dutchman will be any number of scenes prior. So the "conflict" of Act 3 is manufactured and unbelievable, at least by 21st century standards. On the other hand, "Il trovatore" and "La sonnambula" hardly rate a 10 on the credibility scale, so why carp, right? Better if you just go along with the whole male-chorus-getting-shot-with arrows bit -- yes, you read that right -- and not ask too many questions. Bryn Terfel's Dutchman, anyway, is the raison d'être for this filming in the first place, and he's absolutely splendid; no big surprise, but greatly to be appreciated. Equally good are the Daland of opera great Matti Salminen and, in a much smaller role, the Helmsman of Fabio Trümpy. Less successful, IMHO, are Anja Kampe, who's a little shrill in the upper register and Marco Jentzsch's callow, strident Erik. Bottom line: This cockeyed, crazy interpretation of "Der fliegende Holländer" maybe not be ideal, but until another, more conventional version with Terfel comes along, it will just have to do. But if you can't stomach the unconventional, and it will interfere with your ability to enjoy the singing, stay far, far away.

history.title: Asagaroff, Grischa - Cavalleria Rusticana/pagliacci [Blu-ray]
history.text: This is a 2008, no-frills "Cav & Pag," built around solid dual performances by Argentine tenor José Cura. Also well served are the sizzling Santuzza of Paoletta Marrocu and the Silvio of barihunk Gabriel Bermudez. Director Grischa Asagaroff makes some odd, detrimental choices, some small (there was certainly no breakdancing in the 1940s), some not-so-small (having Lola live directly next door to Tiriddu in "Cavalleria Rusticana" makes no dramatic sense whatsoever, as well as contradicts the libretto); otherwise this is a safe, unimaginatively staged production. At this price, though, why would you not make the investment?

history.title: Mascagni: Cavalleria Rusticana - Leoncavallo: Pagliacci
history.text: Jonas Kaufmann is, as expected, riveting in his role debuts as Turiddu and Canio in this production of "Cav" & "Pag" from the 2015 Salzburg Easter festival. As he has demonstrated over and over again, he is the full package, one seemingly designed by the gods for the HD age of opera: ridiculously handsome, with a glorious voice and the acting chops of Brando. Unfortunately, the production, by German film director Philipp Stölzl, lets him and the rest of the fine cast down in a big way. The concept, which presents both pieces as if they were some sort of living comic strip, complete with a stage awkwardly divided into frames, and bizarre, almost surreal, sets and costumes, is the antithesis of "verismo," the movement for which these operas are the prime examples. Many of the directorial choices are jarring and senseless -- Turiddu and Santuzza having a son of 8 or 9 years old, Mamma Lucia being some kind of underworld money launderer (!), Tonio apologizing for presenting himself to the audience "alone" when he's in fact surrounded by the entire cast, Canio slapping an annoying child at the top of "Pagliacci"-- but in the world of regietheater, can one expect anything else? Well, yes. I'm not against updating and high concept, by any means, but the arbitrariness of what Stölzl is doing here just ends up being claustrophobic and distracting. I will not be keeping this video in my collection. Kaufmann has been just as good elsewhere, and there will be, hopefully, a better "Cav" & "Pag" in future with which to replace it.

history.title: The Lost City of Z
history.text: This film is as slow as Percy Fawcett's expeditions to South America. The performances are dull, and the cinematography muddy and oddly greenish at times. The angles at which the director often chooses to shoot are mystifying and without point. An exciting story told in a plodding, amateurish manner. All in all, a frustrating miss.

history.review_title: If you like "Peanuts", you should like this one.
history.text: Like many people, I was skeptical about this movie when I first heard about it. Charles Schulz has been dead and gone these sixteen years. How could a new "Peanuts" movie possibly retain the spirit of the original comic strip? I must say I was very pleasantly surprised. The computer animation takes some getting used to (for those of us that grew up on the classic "Peanuts" animation), but I thought the storyline was compelling enough. It's basically an expanded version of the "You're in Love, Charlie Brown" special from the late 1960's. Charlie Brown is enamored with the Little Red-Haired Girl, and he makes all kinds of attempts to impress her. Of course, he inevitably makes a fool of himself every time. I won't spoil it by giving away the ending, but it's a happy one. The movie also contains a subplot that involves two of Snoopy's best-known personas: the world-famous novelist and the World War I flying ace. Snoopy is writing a love story in which he imagines himself as a World War I pilot. Between his attempts to rescue his sweetheart (an unnamed female beagle), he has run-ins with the infamous Red Baron. It's probably not as funny as his adventures in the comic strip, but it's still pretty good. I've been a "Peanuts" fan for more than forty years, and I've seen every one of their feature films. "Race For Your Life, Charlie Brown" is still my favorite, but this one may very well come in second. I just wish they'd given it a more creative title.

history.title: Snow White and the Three Stooges
history.review_title: Zzzzzz.... Huh? What was the name of this movie again?
history.text: At the time this movie was made, the Three Stooges were at the height of their popularity. Children were their greatest fans, and every school child knows the story of Snow White, so why not bring the two together? Instead of having Snow White be rescued and assisted by seven bumbling dwarfs, why not let her be rescued and assisted by the three greatest bumblers in the history of Hollywood? It sounded like a can't-miss idea at the time. For good measure, why not throw in a big budget, a grandiose musical score, several impressive skating scenes, all under the direction of the great Walter Lang? What could possibly go wrong with a movie like that? In fact, plenty did go wrong. Moe Howard later wrote, "We Stooges had never been in such an expensive film." He was glad they had opted for a straight salary instead of a percentage, because the latter option would not have paid well. Why did this movie do so poorly? For one thing, it contains entirely too much pageantry. Carol Heiss did a decent job as Snow White, but many of the scenes and dance numbers serve absolutely no purpose other than to show off her talents as a figure skater. Besides, there were just too many of them. The overkill on the music and skating left the Stooges with relatively little screen time, and they were the main drawing card. The Stooges did a creditable job in their performances. They did some funny scenes, and they showed some genuine pathos when the script called for it. Alas, their scenes were too few and far between. The Stooges' black-and-white films from this era are not as impressive in terms of cinematography, but they're much funnier and more entertaining. Personally, I would stick with those. Better yet, why not seek out some of their classic two-reel films from the 30's and 40's? Those are really the vintage Stooges. As for this movie, I would only recommend it as a cure for your insomnia.

history.title: The Three Stooges: Stop! Look! and Laugh!
history.review_title: An okay movie, but the story behind it is the most interesting part.
history.text: I saw this movie when I was a kid and liked it. Even as an adult, I think it has plenty of positive qualities, though it's not terribly creative. It's basically a hodgepodge of clips from the classic Three Stooges comedies. These clips, alas, are not as funny as the original versions, largely because of the annoying background music that the producers chose to dub in for no apparent reason. In between are some very funny scenes involving Paul Winchell and his "friends", Jerry Mahoney and Knucklehead Smiff. In my opinion, these are the best parts of the movie. The story behind the movie is more interesting than the movie itself. The truth is, Columbia Pictures treated the Stooges very poorly. They worked for Columbia for twenty-four years. During that time they never got a raise, and when the old movies were released to television, the Stooges were shut out of receiving any royalties. Ironically, the release of these films was the best thing that ever happened to the Stooges, because it brought them a new wave of popularity. Columbia Pictures starred them in a feature film called "Have Rocket, Will Travel". It was so successful that Columbia wanted them to make a second feature, but this time the Stooges had other ideas. They had formed their own production company, and they wanted to make "The Three Stooges Meet Hercules" as their next picture. Since Columbia couldn't get the Stooges to star in a new movie, they decided to make one without them, and the result was "Stop! Look! And Laugh!" Alas, Columbia didn't realize that things had changed since the old days. The Stooges were aware of their new popularity, and they no longer took kindly to being exploited. Citing "unfair competition", they took the matter to court and obtained an injunction prohibiting Columbia from releasing the movie. Columbia apologized to the Stooges, and they agreed to a compromise: they would be allowed to release "Stop! Look! And Laugh!", and in exchange they would finance "The Three Stooges Meet Hercules." The latter picture was a huge hit, and Columbia financed three more pictures for the Stooges, but this time the Stooges were in the driver's seat. Columbia's days of exploiting them were officially over!

history.review_title: One of John Wayne's most underrated movies.
history.text: I disagree with those who dismiss this movie as just another jingoistic war picture. Next to "The Sands of Iwo Jima" and perhaps "The Fighting Seabees", I consider this one of John Wayne's best war movies. I grant that the cinematography and the writing could have been better, but the dichotomy between the two lead characters is enough to hold my fascination. John Wayne plays Major Daniel Kirby, who has just taken over command of a squadron of newly-minted fighter pilots. Robert Ryan plays his executive officer, Captain Carl "Griff" Griffin. Griff served as exec under the preceding commander, and his men are surprised when he's not appointed as the new commander. The squadron soon gets orders to leave for Guadalcanal, where they get their first taste of combat. Dan and Griff get along well enough at first, but tensions begin to mount as their differences in personality and leadership style begin to surface. Dan seems cold and callous in his willingness to send men to their deaths. Griff, by contrast, is much more compassionate toward the men, but his compassion gets in the way of his ability to make tough decisions, and Dan considers him an ineffective leader. In fact, Dan loathes the realities of combat as much as Griff, but he understands it's part of the job. No doubt he shares the sentiment expressed by General George Patton: "Every commander, no matter what his rank, has to send to certain death every day a certain number of men. Some of them are his personal friends; all of them are his personal responsibility. Any man with a heart would want to sit down and bawl like a baby, but [a commander] can't, so he sticks out his jaw and swaggers and swears." [SPOILER ALERT] By the movie's end, Dan and Griff gain a new respect for each other. Griff has to make a difficult decision that results in the death of his closest friend. As a result, he is able to see things from Dan's perspective. Meanwhile Dan is relieved of command due to combat injuries, and upon his recommendation, Griff takes over as the new commander. As Dan boards his plane to leave for the States, he reminds Griff that combat command is a very stressful and lonely job. If you like a movie that keeps a good balance between patriotism and the harsh realities of war, I highly recommend "The Flying Leathernecks".

history.title: They Died With Their Boots On
history.review_title: In the words of Jed Clampett, "Pitiful! Just pitiful!"
history.text: Most movies about history contain inaccuracies, some more than others. "They Died With Their Boots On" may have some value as entertainment, but when it comes to historical inaccuracy, this one really scrapes the proverbial bottom of the barrel. It came on TCM yesterday and I watched about an hour of it. It was so twisted I could hardly stomach it. Did the writers of this screenplay not do any research at all? Let me give you just a few examples. The movie opens with Custer arriving as a cadet at West Point in 1857. It gives the impression that he is a wealthy aristocrat (Custer actually came from a rather modest family). He is nearly kicked out of the Academy, but is rescued by the superintendent, Col. Philip Sheridan (Sheridan was never superintendent of West Point, and in 1857 he was an unknown lieutenant serving in the Oregon territory). As a cadet, Custer constantly gets into trouble for his undisciplined behavior, and his record is "even worse than Ulysses S. Grant" (Grant finished near the middle of his class, while Custer was at the very bottom of his). Later, Custer becomes a cavalryman and, evidently, leads his men to victory at the First Battle of Bull Run (Hello! The Union lost that battle, and the territory on the screen looks awfully arid for northern Virginia). The movie depicts Gen. Winfield Scott as commander of the Union army long after the Civil War ends (he retired shortly after the war began and died in 1866). As I said, these are just a few of the inaccuracies. When the movie gets to Custer's career after the war, it REALLY starts playing fast-and-loose with the truth. For instance, it shows Custer drowning his sorrows with alcohol (Custer swore off drinking during the war, and never touched alcohol for the rest of his life). It also depicts him having a peace conference with Crazy Horse (Crazy Horse never negotiated with whites) in which the famed chief offers to turn over all Indian lands except the Black Hills (in the words of the younger generation, "As if!"). It also gives the impression that Custer really wanted to make peace with the Sioux (again, "As if!"). Alas, Custer's efforts at peace are thwarted when some dirty rotten scoundrels spread a rumor that gold has been found in the Black Hills (actually, that rumor was started by only one dirty rotten scoundrel, and his name was George Custer). I can respect people watching this movie because they're fans of Errol Flynn and Olivia de Haviland. They did the best they could in spite of the mediocre writing. If you're looking for a lesson in history, though, avoid this movie like the proverbial plague.

history.title: Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory
history.review_title: It has its good points and bad points.
history.text: Many people consider this movie an all-time classic. It was based on Roald Dahl's "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory". When I was little, I read the book before I saw the movie, so I was disappointed by the liberties it took with the plot. As an adult, I've tried to view the movie more objectively, and I'll admit it has a number of good points. Gene Wilder was quite good as Willy Wonka. He portrayed the character pretty much like he was presented in the book - quirky, but not creepy. In fact, I didn't really come to appreciate Wilder's performance until I saw Johnny Depp's attempt to play the same character (Depp's portrayal of Wonka was VERY creepy. I can't imagine any self-respecting parent wanting their children to be around a guy like that). The movie also has a number of delightful songs, such as "The Candy Man" and "Pure Imagination". The songs are nicely spaced so they don't drag down the plot (unlike "Pete's Dragon", which was a musical overkill). I also thought Jack Albertson was a fine choice to play Grandpa Joe. As I said, the movie takes a number of liberties with the plot of the book. Some of them are understandable. For instance, Charlie's mother was not a widow in the book, and I suspect the screenplay writers added this element to give the movie some extra pathos. Also, Mr. Slugworth was not a major character in the book (he was only mentioned a couple of times in passing, along with a couple of Wonka's other competitors). His appearances in the movie added an element of mystery that kept the plot moving along. Also, though Gene Wilder gave a fine performance, he was much too young to play Willy Wonka (so was Johnny Depp). In the book, Wonka was a much older man. My biggest quarrel with the movie is the scene where Charlie and Grandpa Joe steal some of Wonka's "fizzy lifting drinks". It's a funny scene, but it completely goes against the spirit of the book. In the book, Charlie was awarded the chocolate factory because he obeyed Mr. Wonka's instructions and was not self-willed like the other children. By adding this element, the writers made Charlie as naughty as the other kids. Be that as it may, I still think "Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory" has enough good points to make it worth the viewing. However, if you read the book, I think you'll agree that it's much better than both of the film versions.

history.title: The Shakiest Gun in the West
history.review_title: Not as good as "The Paleface", but still pretty good.
history.text: This was a remake of Bob Hope's classic "The Paleface". Don Knotts was a talented comedian and played his part well, but I don't think he played it as well as Hope did. Also, the overall movie is just not as well-made as "The Paleface". That being said, this is still a pretty good movie in its own right. View both of them and judge for yourself.

history.title: Yearling, The
history.review_title: A good movie, but not as good as the book.
history.text: I first saw this movie when I was little. It's funny in some points, and sad in others. Still, I like the book a lot better. The cast is good. Claude Jarman, Jr., was a fine choice to play young Jody Baxter, and he looks pretty much the way Jody is described in the book. Jane Wyman also did a creditable job as Ora Baxter, Jody's mother, but she was a bit too petite (in the book, Ora was a rather buxom woman). Gregory Peck was undoubtedly a fine actor, but he was all wrong for the part of Jody's father, Ezra "Penny" Baxter. The book explains that he was nicknamed "Penny" because of his diminutive size. Peck was 6'3", so he didn't exactly look the part. The movie's plot is generally faithful to the book, but it doesn't bring out the book's theme all that well. The book was about more than a boy and his pet fawn. It was about the harsh realities of life on the frontier. Young Jody is gradually introduced to some of the harsher aspects of life, such as death, crop failure, storms, and disease. These harsh realities eventually threaten Jody's relationship with his pet fawn (you'll have to see the movie or read the book to find out). In fact, the title has kind of a double meaning. A yearling is an animal that is between the stages of infancy and adulthood, so the title describes Jody as well as his pet. These elements aside, "The Yearling" is a good family movie, and I highly recommend it. However, I also recommend you read the book, too, and I think you'll like it even better. Even so, I must say the movie added one scene at the end that I thought was an improvement. The book and the movie both depict Ora Baxter as an emotionally cold woman. She has already buried several children, so she is either unable or unwilling to show Jody affection. In the last scene of the movie, Jody learns that his mother does indeed love him. That's all I'm going to tell you. You'll have to watch the movie to find out!

history.title: The Frog Prince
history.review_title: One of Jim Henson's earlier projects, but still one of his best.
history.text: I was just four years old when this special first aired on television in 1971. "Sesame Street" was still a new phenomenon in those days, and so were Jim Henson's Muppets. This was one of Henson's first independent productions and, in my opinion, it's still one of his best. Kermit the Frog narrates the story as an observer. It depicts him living in a well near an old castle, and he meets a small frog named Robin (yes, it's the same frog who later played Kermit's nephew). Robin claims his real name is Sir Robin the Brave, and that he's actually a handsome prince. He tells of a witch who cast a spell on him, and the only way he can break the spell is if a princess befriends and kisses him. Kermit and the other frogs are skepitical, of course, but Kermit befriends Robin anyway and welcomes him to the well. Robin soon learns that a princess lives in the nearby castle, and he is determined to meet her. However, he soon learns that the witch who turned him into a frog is also living in the castle - posing as the king's sister, no less - and has put a spell on the princess. The witch recognizes Robin, and is determined to feed him to an ogre (this was also the first appearance of another well-known character from "The Muppet Show": the lovable Sweetums). Will Robin be fed to the ogre before he's kissed by the princess? Will the princess also be released from her spell? And how did a wicked witch come to live in the palace? Watch the movie and find out! The puppetry is somewhat crude in comparison to Jim Henson's later projects, but it still contains all the elements of a good Muppet production: an exciting story line, funny dialogue, and catchy songs. I recommend it for people of all ages.

"The Birth of a Nation" is an important piece of cinema history in itself. It was the first motion picture to employ such techniques as closeups, long shots, and careful film editing. Someone has rightly said that it transformed movies from a novelty into an art form. Nevertheless, the movie has been justifiably criticized by civil rights groups for its negative depiction of African-Americans and its sympathetic portrayal of the Ku Klux Klan. The movie is set during the Civil War and the Reconstruction era that followed, and it focuses on the trials and tribulations of different people. The main characters are fictional, but they are based on real people. The first half of the movie focuses on the war, and it's not that bad. It is heavily biased toward the South and is loaded with racial stereotypes, but it's not any worse than "Gone With the Wind" in those areas. Its depiction of Abraham Lincoln's assassination is remarkably accurate, and it also correctly depicts the South's reaction to his death. John Wilkes Booth did not do the South any favors when he killed Lincoln. Whatever faults Lincoln might have had, vindictiveness was not one of them, and he favored easy and compassionate peace terms toward the former Confederate states. When Lincoln was killed, the South was left at the mercy of Andrew Johnson and the Radical Republicans. Unfortunately, neither had much mercy to show. The second half of the movie focuses on the Reconstruction era, and that's the part that aroused the most controversy. This is where the movie goes beyond racial stereotypes into out-and-out racism. It depicts newly freed slaves taking over state governments and making a mockery of government and justice, until finally the "heroic" Ku Klux Klan comes to the rescue. I am a white southerner, and I agree that much of the Reconstruction policy in the South was harsh and unfair. However, it is equally unfair to place this level of blame on former slaves, most of whom wanted nothing more than to enjoy their new rights as American citizens. As I said, "The Birth of a Nation" is an important piece of movie history, but its depiction of history is terrible. I encourage people to view it , not to learn about the Civil War and Reconstruction, but to learn more about racial attitudes in our nation in the early 20th century.
