history.title: CARMEN.maquia and Club Havana [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: A stunner... where can I see more of this choreographer and this company?
history.text: Wow, wow, and triple wow. Gustavo Ramirez Sansano's "Carmen.manquia" is neither ballet (no classical positions, movements, or pointe work) nor conventional modern dance (too many emotionally intense ballet-like, pas de deux-like male-female interactions). Sansano in effect invents a new kind of dance---more agitatedly, anxiously kinetic and physically embodied than most ballet, but more intimately, privately, emotionally intense, personally interactive, and deeply romantic than most modern dance--and what a stunner of an invention!!! "Carmen.manquia" is one of the most emotionally moving and artistically astonishing dance pieces (ably filmed by Matthew Diamond and edited by Garish Bhargava, the two best in the biz) I have seen in years. A re-telling of the Carmen story to a medley of Bizet music, including the Andante movement from "Symphony in C," -- ah, at the sound of the first blended harmonies George Balanchine's ghost materializes in the background, but with what a shocking artistic transformation transpiring in the foreground -- which becomes the backing for one of the many miraculously inventive, delightfully protracted, and completey unBalanchine-like pas de deuxes between baby-faced Christopher Bloom and hotter than a tamale Kimberly Van Woesik. If you don't know Bizet's Carmen, you'll be at a slight disadvantage but can still get by since there are intertitles to help you, though your enjoyment will be increased if you are familiar with the original so you can appreciate what Sansano has done to shake it up. Highly, highly recommended for fans of both ballet and modern dance. (The shorter curtain-closer by Pedro Ruiz is more conventional and emotionally better behaved, but you'll need a chance to catch your breath after the opening piece anyway.) Ballet Hispanico is a company to watch in coming years.

history.title: The Cherry Orchard
history.review_title: Whatever it is, this is not Chekhov
history.text: The reviews here generally fall into two categories: 1) I love Chekhov's "ensemble" "talky" "interactional" plays, therefore I love this movie; or 2) I find Chekhov's kind of drama tedious, pointless, and non-cinematic, therefore I hate this movie. The truth is neither. And sadder. I adore Chekhov's work. I know and have seen live on stage, on BBC TV, or on film every play many many times, and more or less every major film and video production. Chekhov is a genius. There is no question about that. So much for objection number 2. Those folks are simply philistines who can't appreciate subtle imaginative interaction. But number 1 is not right either. This film bears almost NO relation to what Chekhov wrote or to any performance of The Cherry Orchard that has ever been staged. It has been totally re-written and reconstructed by the writer-director, and completely transformed in unChekovian ways to turn it into a movie. Not a single Chekhovian scene, interaction, speech, or play of personality survives. So the number 1 folks, who mistake this for Chekhov's The Cherry Orchard are wrong too. This movie has nothing to do with Chekhov's play beyond the title, the plot, the characters' names, and the setting. It is just a bad movie. Go rent or buy a video that has the actual play on it. (The BBC and Royal Shakespeare Company productions available on this site are excellent.) Go to a local theatre and catch a live performance. Go onto YouTube or some internet site that has a grainy, pixilated, postage-stamp version of the play to view. Any or all of these things will at least give you a glimmering of what Chekhov looks and sounds like. A glimpse of his genius. You are free to like it or dislike it, as you please, though if you don't appreciate it, never forget that that is almost certainly your fault, not the fault of the production. At least what you will find in those other ways will be Chekhov. That's not what this is. You won't find a trace of the real Chekhov in this film--only (as I say) a few characters with the same names, the bare bones of the same plot, and a bunch of cherry trees in an orchard (cherry trees which are invisible and merely imaginary in the actual play, a not unimportant difference). None of those things has anything to do with Chekhov's play or genius, which you won't find a trace of here. Just banality and literal-mindedness and movie-star (which is to say, fake) drama.

history.title: Anton Chekhov Collection (Platonov/The Wood Demon/The Proposal/The Wedding/The Seagull/An Artist's Story/Uncle Vanya [1970 and 1991 versions]/Three Sisters/The Cherry Orchard [1962 and 1981 versions])
history.review_title: The greatest playwright of the past 400 years and a set to cherish, live with, live into, and learn from
history.text: Almost universally superb productions of all of the plays, including Chekhov's juvenilia. The Platonov production is particuarly wonderful, given the infrequency with which it is attempted; and the productions of the major plays are among the best ever recorded on film. The adaptations of the short stories are less successful. But don't let that make you hesitate. Chekhov is, beyond doubt or dispute, the most important dramatist, in any language or culture, since Shakespeare. The most important dramatist of the past four hundred years. No cultured person (as few of them as there may be at this point in the history of world) can afford to live and die without having grappled and come to grips with, and been enlighted by, his work. It is possible to do this by buying a cheap translation and reading the plays. (If that is your path, I recommend the Ronald Hingley translation of the major plays, available on this site in an inexpensive paperback edition. The introduction alone is worth the price of the volume.) But this is the hard way to encounter Chekhov. The wrong way. You would have to be a genius, and a dedicated, devoted genius to master the plays this way, if you have never seen them acted. The right way, the easy way, the sublime way, is to view actual productions where you have the thinking of the greatest actors and directors to guide you. And that is where this set of DVDs comes in. You can have A+ versions of ALL of the major plays, in several cases more than one production of a play, in a single compact set, for a song. This is a set to live with and learn from over the years. Thank Gosh for the BBC and their "Play of the Month" series, which picked top-flight directors, assembled all-star casts (read the credits, they're a who's who of the greats of 1960s-1990s British acting), and backed the whole thing financially. It couldn't ever happen in America, on American TV or in American film--and it didn't. (Look at the sheer awfulness of what American movie-makers and TV adapters did to Tennessee Williams' work. Too embarrassing to talk about.) HIghly highly recommended.

history.title: Petipa, Marius - Don Quichot
history.review_title: Light comedy, mostly (merely) acrobatic dancing, emotional shallowness, but not bad as entertainment
history.text: I've heard about Alexi Ratmansky's work for four or five years now, but this was the first piece of his I've actually seen. Not bad. A light comic presentation at the divertissement level (there is not a single emotionally deep or choreographically complex pas de deux in the entire piece), but as I say not bad. Ratmansky is especially good with group/corps de ballet work, and even better with pairings of dancers dancing more or less in synchrony. The dancing in this production is top-flight. Matthew Golding (as Basilio here) is always worth watching and Anna Tsygankova (as Kitri) is just plain superb (a major-league turner and kicker), as are Maiko Tsutsumi and Nadia Yanowsky (playing a paired female duo, and doing exceptionally strong dancing, really almost as good as the principals). Beyond the lightness of the semi-comic tone, the weakness, of course, is the Minkus music, which never rises above the level of being "entertaining," and that is perhaps why there is so little emotional depth to the Basilio-Kitri partnering, though I do think Ratmansky might have tried to do more with Minkus choreographically. (Balanchine showed that even Gershwin and Sousa could be turned into interesting dance, not to mention Delibes with his Coppelia.) There is one real choreographic blooper, however, that I hope Ratmansky doesn't repeat. During Quixote's Dream in the second half of the second act, Ratmansky has the hammy actor playing the Don mug and gesticulate in the background behind the principals as they dance. Tres distracting! Trop silly! Quel dommage! A big mistake, Alexi. Let the dancers hold the stage uncontested. Let us be able to pay attention to them--not be distracted by an old man mugging behind them. This is ballet after all, not cinema-verite. We all know that it's Quixote's Dream. You don't have to have the Don waving his arms and making faces while the Queen of the Dryads and Cupid and others are busting their chops dancing in front of him. There are also some bloopers in the television camera work and editing where shots of minor characters reacting to what is going on are intercut into major dance sequences five or six times, when we are just dying to see the dancers and steps. Perhaps they are there to cover brief gaps in the footage. But the video production is otherwise technically satisfactory. The sound is generally well-balanced (with just a few exceptions when the orchestra is mixed-in too loud, a common problem on Blu-Rays) and the image (when it doesn't cut to a background figure) is sharp and well-lighted (differently lighted than a stage production, as it must be for video). In summary, as long as you don't expect more than Nutcracker level light comedy (but sans anything to compare even remotely with the depth, seriousness, and choreographic complexity of the Nutcracker's final act Grand Pas de Deux, and as long as you don't mind Minkus's rather foursquare music, which never comes within a thousand miles of the emotional impact of Tchaikovsky's), you won't be disappointed. I am glad to have this on Blu-Ray for a light evening's entertainment.

history.title: Handel: Alcina & Tamerlano
history.review_title: Satisifying and respectful productions, about the music and performances, not the fake brilliance of the stage-director
history.text: In an era in which it seems that virtually every other Handel opera is mounted in a "deconstructed," "high-concept" production, in which some of the most heart-rending, tormented, exultant, heroic performances in all of opera are transformed by the stage director into forms of po-mo camp and put-on, in which sopranos are costumed in cellophane blouses and purple mini-skirts and tenors are forced to wear funny hats and circus bloomers, these productions (beautifully mounted by Christophe Rousset) are the rarest of rarities--ones that respect the text and understand that to hear the singing and music and to vibrate to the genius of the composer are why we bought our ticket or purchased the disk. Pierre Audi's one indulgence is not really an indulgence at all. While a given singer is performing he will have the character or characters they are singing about make an entrance behind them and allow the two or three of them to exchange glances or silently interact. This is not in Handel's text, and was no doubt not in his mise-en-scene, but it does not trample on his intentions the way the opera-as-circus-performance, post-modern, high concept form of production does. It simply gives us a little more to look at and livens up the interest of the stage performances a tad by having a few more characters present on stage at any given moment. I highly recommend this set--two quite different operas, one from fairly early in Handel's opera-writing career (Tamerano, unfortunately not a work of the first rank), and one from near the end (Alcina, one of his musically most fascinating works), totalling more than six hours of running time in all, mounted in unostentatiously respectful and beautifully sung productions with good shot choices and impeccable sound (in both 2-channel PCM and 5.1 DTS). What's not to like? If you want circus performances, practically any other Handel production available on this site will do. Or better yet, just buy a ticket to see the clowns and trapeze artists. They'll actually be a lot more interesting (and funnier) than most of the terminally silly and lethally unfunny kitsch productions that have been mounted.

history.title: Helen Mirren at the BBC (The Changeling / The Apple Cart / Caesar and Claretta / The Philanthropist / The Little Minister / The Country Wife / Blue Remembered Hills / Mrs. Reinhardt / Soft Targets)
history.text: I wanted to love the content, but alas, much of it is not accessible, not viewable or listenable. There are serious manufacturing errors in the disks that make much of their content inaccessible (you click on the menu choices and nothing and I mean nothing happens; you can't get past the menu) or only partially accessible (you get halfway or a little more than halfway through a play and the picture and sound seize up/freeze so bad you have to force-eject the disk to get out of it, and get it out, only to have the problem repeat over and over again, so that no matter how you try to jump past or skip the supposed "bad spot," you can never see the final half hour (or whatever) of the work. I am a media professional with high-end equipment and multiple disk players and nothing will play many of these selections and no amount of cleverness on my part can over-ride the problems. This is not a "single bad disk" issue caused by dirt, fingerprints, or scratches; it is a disk coding and manufacturing issue that affects many apparently pristine and unplayed disks in many different places. Be forewarned. You will be very frustrated.

history.title: Mendelssohn: A Midsummer Night's Dream [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Telling the dancer from the dance
history.text: What a time machine watching this was. I haven't seen it since Suzanne Farrell danced Titania and Jacques d'Amboise or Jean-Pierre Bonnefoux played Puck on the stage of the State Theater. The costumes have been updated (the children/fairies/butterflies much brighter--perhaps a bit too brightly bedecked in terms of their wigs!--but not bad overall) and the two pairs of confused, mismatched lovers given color-coded garb to make keeping them straight a little easier to do; but according to the booklet at least (I can't trust my memory on this one), not a step has been altered. It is otherwise exactly as George Balanchine created it. For the sake of old times (and in honor of Balanchine's memory), I wanted to love everything about this production, but alas, it takes more than brighter costumes and historically-correct choreography (assuming that is actually the case) to make a ballet, just as it takes more than playing the right notes to make music. There is the imagination, the virtuosity, the daring of the performer and the performance, in both cases, and the Pacific Northwest Ballet just can't cut it. Passages of corps-work that I remember as contrapuntally dazzling and stunningly intricate look merely rushed and crowded (is the stage also too small?)--bodies moving in every direction, busy enough to hold your attention and excite your emotions, but not enough to delight your mind in the Balanchine way. Mere busyness cannot take the place of miracles of timing and ingenuity. Even the two strongest dancers in the company (to my eyes at least), Patricia Barber as Titania and Lisa Apple as Helena, never quite bring their performances into focus. It's a real lesson in how the steps are not enough to make a performance. The New York City Ballet (and Farrell in particular it goes without saying) brought daring, emotional extremity, and imaginative significance to their performances, in this ballet and every other one they danced, while these dancers (all of them, not just the two I mentioned) are doing steps, not exciting us with their presence, their allure, their relationship with their partner. There was a minute or two (in Helena's first Kenneth-MacMillan-like fight scene) when I thought Lisa Apple was going to break through the choreography and give me real emotional anguish and desperation, and another minute or two (in a late first-act pas de deux for Titania) when I thought Patricia Barker was going to give me Farrell-like emotional intensity, instabilty, unpredictability, or scarey imbalance, but the minute or two in each case came and went and left no emotional ripples in its wake and the dancing dropped back into being a series of technical steps, mechanical movements, and athletic extensions. The choreography of Midsummer Night's Dream is something still to be conquered in a filmed production, and preserving the historical accuracy of the steps will not be enough to do it. It will require performers who can bring the steps to life--to make them emotionally matter--and that will take courage, daring, virtuosity--and most of all thought, about the meaning of the solos and partnerings and movements. Dance is meaning; dance tells us things about our lives and relationships. Dance is not steps. Yeats was wrong. There is a cosmic difference between the realms: The dancer has to create the dance; it is not already there in the choreography.

history.title: La Bete et la Belle
history.text: I only discovered the work of Toulouse-based French choreographer Kader Belarbi in the past year. He is one of the best-kept secrets in the worlds of both ballet and modern dance. He works in both forms of expression, often mixing them, and this piece is an example of the modern dance side of his brain. This whole dance is a wonder, with the pas de deux between Beauty and Beast that conclude Acts 1 and 2 being particularly fine. It's not hard to recommend purchase of this work. But for an even greater bargain, note that three of Belarbi's evening-length dances, La Bete et la Belle, La Reine Morte, and La Corsaire, are available together in one set for a song. You can buy all three of them packaged together, in either Blu-Ray or DVD, on this site, for roughly the price of any one of the titles purchased individually. American Ballet Theater and New York City Ballet should give him a ring. He's a major talent. Let's bring him to America. We need him.

history.title: L.M. Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables: DVD (2016)
history.text: As the reviews show, opinion is split on this version. On one side are those who grew up with the book (and its sequels) and came to the DVD looking for a video re-creation of their memory of reading Anne of Green Gables when they were 10 or 12. They want something faithful and true to the written text. This is the wrong DVD for that. If you want a re-creation of the book, you will be disappointed since this 90-minute presentation only picks out eight or ten brief episodes (almost entirely from the first half of the book) and dispenses with the rest. On the other side are viewers like me, who either have not read the book or, like me, are willing to judge the video on its own merits, as an independent and free-standing creation. If you can do that, if you do not have a mental-checklist of how you think the book should have been filmed, you will not be disappointed. This is a beautifully touching presentation--if you can simply treat it as the story of episodes in a young girl's life and her effect on three adults and a few childhood friends who love her. Regarded this way, this is a completely fulfilling cinematic experience in its own right. I've at this point watched this film twice with the same result. To my complete astonishment, since it happens so rarely when I am watching a film, my eyes welled over with tears at some point in virtually every scene and by the end I was silently sobbing throughout the final minutes--embarrassed at the intensity of my own feelings, even as a different analytic part of my mind wondered at how the effect was achieved. I might as well add that I'm a man, and a fairly sophisticated one (a film professor), and that there are very few serious, adult-level films that do this to me, which makes me marvel all the more at how beautifully crafted this work is. In short, if you can put the book out of your mind for long enough to watch this, this DVD offers a very wonderful experience--for a child or for the child in all of us.

history.title: Tutto Puccini: Boxed Set
history.review_title: Several of historical value, a few up to contemporary recording standards
history.text: Note that in several of these operas you are not getting contemporary, up-to-date high-def recordings but archival, poor quality transfers of operas performed and recorded in the 1980s or thereabouts that have been "upscaled" onto Blu Ray disks. (The worst are the Sister Angelica and Johnny Sichi recordings, which are from the 1950s and unsubtitled, I believe.) In short, in about a third of these performances the images are fuzzy, poorly lighted, and low resolution. If you are listening to opera for the voices, there are some good moments to be had on the PCM tracks (same as CD quality), but if you expect anything resembling video recordings made in the past 20 years, you will (with three or four exceptions) be crest-fallen, as I was. (Note that the image of the album back on the Amazon listing page appears to be deliberately reduced in size to prevent you from reading the recording dates of a number of these productions. And beware of reviewers who don't reveal the age of many of these recordings. They are almost certainly employees of one of the companies that is selling this set, or devotees of antique performances.)

history.title: The Dictator - BANNED & UNRATED Version
history.review_title: He should have stuck with his formula
history.text: I admit that I enjoyed [[ASIN:B009EE87NK Borat]]. It was original, truly funny in many places, and provided an uncomfortable insight into several aspects of the American character. Cohen's follow-up [[ASIN:B002TL08FU Brüno]], however, fell flat as it was essentially the same joke - an outrageous foreigner playing the unsuspecting locals for saps, but to make an impression on audiences, it had to be even more over-the-top and ridiculous. It failed because it was trying too hard and was too self-conscious. Fortunately, Cohen is now too well known to be able to pull off yet another stunt in that vein, so he abandoned it in favor of a straight-up comedy. The result isn't much better, and while it might have been possible to fool enough people into playing along with the possibility that they were meeting a real, deposed Middle Eastern dictator, we instead have a script that plays it safe by trying to mimic the results of improvisation. This has never worked, and the script that imagines the effect of inflicting a blatantly arrogant, hateful, and misogynistic cretin onto the denizens of New York City comes across as completely unbelievable, especially the love interest that occupies most of the screen time. The convoluted "political" segment of the plot is as ludicrous as can be expected in what is supposed to pass for a comedy, although Cohen manages to squeeze a speech in toward the end that might qualify as social commentary. [[ASIN:B004NWPY7A The Great Dictator]], it's not. Stupid, insulting, and forgettable, "The Dictator" cannot even be recommended to those dedicated to seeing every film ever made.

history.review_title: Nature is beautiful. Civilization is not.
history.text: "Seasons" is not a documentary; in the "making of" featurette, the director describes it as a fable, a story of the natural world told from the perspective of the animals. In most films taking place in this sort of environment, the animals are an afterthought; here, they're front and center, with human beings showing up on the periphery and only gradually taking on a greater role. The photography is jaw-dropping as we race through the forest with a pack of wolves, follow migrating geese, and get right in the faces of birds and other creatures that normally stay far away from humans. This was accomplished not through training, but "imprinting," where the animals became so used to human beings that they pretty much went about their business with no more self-consciousness than if the filmmakers had not been there at all. The goal was to show the animals up close, rather than through telephoto lenses, and in this, the film succeeds completely. It begins with an "80,000 year winter" and as the earth warms up, turns into "the age of the forest." The scenery is that of a wild and primeval Europe. The message is a low-key version of that in [[ASIN:B000068OCS Koyaanisqatsi - Life Out of Balance]], that humanity is a blight upon the purity of Nature, only without the stupendous Philip Glass soundtrack. Animals may be an afterthought in other movies, but the music was definitely an afterthought in this one. So much time and energy must have been expended on filming the animals, that there wasn't much left over for anything else. Worth seeing if you enjoy shots of cute animals (even when the predators kill something, the bloodshed is obscured behind a log or some other obstruction), "Seasons" is a triumph of the art of photography if nothing else.

history.review_title: What a woman must put up with
history.text: This delightful yet cynical film brings the last work of Austen's "juvenilia" to the screen in a spectacular period piece. The jaw-dropping sets vie with the sharp and witty dialog to immerse us in a world disconcertingly similar to our own. Kate Beckinsale stars as Lady Susan Vernon, a beautiful and intelligent widow forced by the rules of her society to focus her considerable talents toward the clever manipulation of everyone around her. She would be doing the same thing today, although in a law office or business setting, but the result would be the same. One criticism of the film is that the actors deliver their lines as if they were performing a cold reading, but the emphasis of talk over action is deliberate. Of course no one talks the way people do in this film - unfortunately. Even Tom Bennett's Sir James Marvin - the perennial dingbat that appears in all of Austen's works - steals every scene he's in with his halting yet enthusiastic delivery of inane observations that leave others stupified. With a well-crafted script (that admittedly drew from some great source material), "Love & Freindship [sic]" is a great addition to the canon of Austen screen adaptations.

A film that Martin Scorcese wanted to make for 25 years, "Silence" is a complex, difficult, and profoundly serious work that steadfastly refuses to answer many of the questions it raises. Telling the story of two 17th century Portuguese priests who travel to Japan to locate their former teacher, who reportedly has become an apostate, it asks whether religious faith is something that can be communicated between people. Japan is described as a "swamp" where the tree of European Christianity cannot grow. I was reminded of a scene in [[ASIN:1573623903 Black Robe]], another film about Christian missionaries in a strange land, where at one point someone asks "what about the converts" to which the response is "there are no converts." Can a religion based on the idea of offenses against and redemption from an invisible, all-powerful, yet very personal deity make sense to people who have no concept of such a deity? But at some point in the past, a Middle Eastern desert religion took root in Portugal - why there and not Japan? Against a backdrop of violent and senseless repression, people manage to maintain their faith, but as it turns out, faith in what? One promise of all religion is that it will improve the believer's life - how were the lives of the villagers improved by their adoption of a foreign religion to which the authorities were implacably hostile? And was that religion, despite its name and familiar images, anything like the Christianity practiced in Portugal? As one man says of the priest who taught him the Portuguese language, "he taught much, but learned nothing." The wretched Kichijiro, who renounces his faith by stepping on an icon ("it's just a formality"), may be the most faithful as he keeps returning for "confession" whenever his guilt overcomes him. He seems to get more out of his shallow Christianity of convenience than anyone else does. Symbols are merely representations, but we imbue them with our own reality, and in that way, they gain value. And a man who defaces a sacred symbol may have outwardly renounced his faith, but no one can see into his heart. The film offers no easy answers to the question of the value of outward religious practice as opposed to a private belief, and the inevitable role of religion as a political activity. Long and even tedious, "Silence" balances the inherent meaninglessness of life against the meaning we give it, whether from ourselves or something ultimately unknowable beyond us.

history.title: Lady Jane
history.text: Although not an accurate historical account of Jane Grey's nine-day reign over England in July of 1553, this film takes that incident as a starting point to examine the use of power to positive ends, and how two completely different people can complement each other. Helena Bonham Carter, in one of her earliest roles (and first starring role) plays Jane, presented as a deeply religious, bookish young girl whose sole interests are prayer and Biblical study. Through the machinations of her father and other noblemen, the dying teenage King Edward VI names her as his successor. She's forced into a marriage of convenience with Guildford Dudley, the son of the Duke of Northumberland, and a dissolute libertine whose main qualifications seem to be his "controllability" and his obvious incompatibility with Jane. We soon learn that Guildford is not a dissipated burnout, but is genuinely frustrated with the limitations of the viciously cruel and stratified society he lives in, where the ruling class, of which he is a member, conspires to keep the common people in hopeless poverty. When Jane, who has been sheltered from this truth her entire life, finally learns how her world is built on injustice, she understands that as queen she has no choice but to address this by ordering the breakup of the large noble estates and their redistribution to the peasantry. If allowed to continue, this would have amounted to a Marxist revolution, only from the top down rather than the bottom up. Instead, the revolution is aborted as the nobles take control. If Jane had had her own Robespierre or Beria, to behead the nobility before they could behead her, the result might have been different. In reality, of course, this never happened - Jane was not overthrown to prevent her from turning medieval England into an anarcho-communist worker's collective, but because the nobility switched their allegiance to Henry VIII's daughter Mary, who had a stronger claim to the throne. Jane was declared a usurper and imprisoned, and executed after Wyatt's Protestant rebellion even though she was not involved in it. The film takes liberties with the historical record to ask what would happen if a completely selfless leader decided to upend the class structure. The depressing conclusion is that even this is impossible, and we are left with the same society we have now.

Asghar Farhadi returns to the theme he explored in [[ASIN:B0094G427S A Separation]]; the effect divorce has on children. "The Past" shows a far more complex and disturbing family dynamic; Berenice Bejo plays a woman who has two daughters from her first marriage, and is getting a divorce from her second husband so she can take up with her lover, whose wife has been in a coma for the past eight months following an unsuccessful suicide attempt. There are no elderly grandparents this time; the young parents and children provide enough drama. Farhadi employs the same claustrophobic framing on display in "A Separation," where the characters are never out in the open, but always boxed in and limited by their immediate surroundings. The first scene, in which Ali Mosaffa meets Bejo in the airport as he returns from Iran to France to complete their divorce, sets the stage for the rest of the film with the device of placing them on opposite sides of a soundproof glass wall - they can see but can't hear each other. An exploration of the harm that unhappy people can inflict on each other, and how much responsibility we bear for others' poor choices, the lesson of "The Past" may be that if you aren't willing or able to commit to someone for life, maybe you shouldn't have children.

history.title: Yi Yi (The Criterion Collection) [Blu-ray]
history.text: I don't pretend to be an expert in Chinese cinema - the only Chinese films I've seen that come to mind are [[ASIN:B000R3BMM0 Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon]], [[ASIN:B000PMFS6O Raise the Red Lantern]], and [[ASIN:B0000B1A4J The Crippled Masters]], which I saw many years ago in Togo, dubbed, I think, in Portuguese. They must have sent the French version to Brazil by mistake. I came across "Yi Yi" on a list of "the greatest films ever made," and in that regard, it's somewhat of a disappointment. There's no real plot, per se; the characters' lives unspool as if a camera were present at the most ordinary moments. A family deals with an elderly grandmother falling suddenly into a coma, a group of business partners must decide on the course to save their struggling company, a teenage girl takes her first cautious steps into romance, and a young boy gradually becomes aware of the larger world around him. There are a few emotional explosions - an attempted suicide, an angry breakup, a petty tyrant of an elementary school teacher - but overall the emotional tone is as muted and subdued as the film's color palette, suggesting comparisons to other mumblecore like [[ASIN:B002SAMMKQ The Puffy Chair]]. Yet it is not an easy or trivial thing to evoke the wider panoply of characters' lives and relationships with a few images and scraps of dialog, and at close to three hours, "Yi Yi" succeeds at this to varying degrees, especially with the main character N.J., whose "revelation" ===================== SPOILER ALERT ===================== after meeting an old lover, consists of musing on how the course of his life would have been different if he'd made different choices. This can either be "universal" in that everyone over the age of sixteen has wondered about that, or trite as in, "yes, Einstein, your life would have been different if you'd married someone else." This is either profound, or as Nietzsche described women, "not even shallow." The ending, where the young boy reads a letter he wrote to his dead grandmother, where he shows his growing awareness of life's beauty and the inevitability of death, is something every adult in the film takes for granted. Whether this is sufficient payoff for the time required to arrive there will depend on the viewer. Although the film takes place in Taipei, there's not much in the way of tradition or culture; the characters and the urban setting could be transplanted almost anywhere - Tel Aviv, Karachi, Montevideo, Cleveland - without much alteration. As a commentary on the human condition, the primary observation is how uniform and interchangeable urban culture has become worldwide in the 21st century.

Unusual in that it takes the form of an animated documentary, "Waltz With Bashir" is also the first feature-length Israeli animated film produced in several decades. It concerns the filmmaker's quest to regain the memories of his participation in the 1982 Lebanon invasion, as a teenager in the IDF. The film alternates between his present-day discussions with his fellow soldiers, and dramatic recollection of the events themselves as he struggles to recall his own role in them and in the Sabra and Shatila massacre of Palestinian civilians by Lebanese Phalangist forces. The soldiers are presented as children, not completely understanding the scope of the conflict or its ultimate goals. The soundtrack includes covers of songs by Cake and others that both augment and comment on the action. The Max Richter score is outstanding, although I was annoyed that obvious allusions to Bach's F-minor concerto, Schubert's E-flat trio, and what I am certain is a passage from [[ASIN:B0027534EU Koyaanisqatsi]] were not credited. Overall, however, "Waltz With Bashir" is both an examination of a specific historical event as well as an exposition of the effect warfare has on both its victims and perpetrators.

history.review_title: Where there's smoke, there's fire, but not in this case
history.text: The filmmaker admits at one point that the subject of UFOs is overwhelmed by at least 90% sensationalist nonsense. He then claims that this is how "the truth" is "hidden" - by turning a valid topic into supermarket tabloid material. His argument is that there is so much information on UFOs and aliens, and so many reasonable people believe in them, that they must really exist. The problem, however, is like religion - there's definitely a lot of discussion about God, and a lot of people believe in him, but there's no objective evidence of his existence. UFOs fall into the same category. We're presented with voluminous evidence of alien contact, craft sightings, "unexplained" phenomena, and a succession of very reasonable specialists who assure us that there can be no doubt. We're then told that "the government" has all of this high-tech, top-secret alien material, that is being used on a daily basis, and that "the media" is under careful control to ensure that none of it gets out - except, of course, that a lot of it does. But there's an explanation for this as well - if UFOlogy can be made to look like it's in the domain of tinfoil-hat conspiracy theorists, "the truth" can be hidden in plain sight. No credible researcher will want to commit career suicide by taking seriously what sounds like nonsense. This becomes a self-perpetuating cycle - as UFO study becomes loonier, fewer people want to touch it. If the only people who report contact with aliens are backwoods types who look like they've never seen a pair of shoes, then no Nobel Laureates will want to touch this subject. Fortunately, Greer himself seems to be protected from retaliation by the powers that be - surely, if anything happened to him, that would create too much suspicion. So we learn that there's a lot of information, and a massive conspiracy to conceal or obfuscate it. But other than a few tantalizing glimpses of the child-sized, almond-eyed "aliens," there's none of the hard, objective proof that would set the matter to rest once and for all. Otherwise, the documentary is well-made, with a good balance between talking heads and action, and voiceover by Giancarlo Esposito, "Gustavo Fring" from "Breaking Bad." The overall professional and dignified presentation might convince a few people, but for the rest of us, "Unacknowledged" is still "nonexistent."

history.title: Rumble: The Indians Who Rocked The World
history.text: A good documentary should present something to the audience that they don't already know about, and "Rumble" definitely succeeds there. I must admit that I had not known that Charley Patton and Jimi Hendrix were Native Americans, and while I was of course familiar with the titular song, I'd never heard of Link Wray, or the equally inspirational Mildred Bailey. The contribution of Native Americans to American popular music - the blues, jazz, and rock & roll - has definitely been overlooked. The problem with this documentary is lack of focus. It's not sure if it wants to be an ethnographic study of Native American music, an elucidation of how traditional music informs popular music, or an overview of popular musicians who just happen to be Native American. While the influence and effect of the two and one-half minute "Rumble" is indisputable - it has that aura of inevitability that some compositions of Beethoven and Mozart have, imparting the sense that one has heard it before, even when one is hearing it for the first time, as if it is part of the essential fabric of the universe. But the song really has no relation to traditional Native music other than the fact that a Native American wrote and performed it. The attempt to characterize the blues as derived from Native American traditional music comes across as wishful thinking, especially since no clear analysis is provided of what the Native music of the Mississippi Delta sounded like. Other examples toward the end of the film seem almost grasping at straws in the attempt to equate an evocation of past tradition with the unbroken continuation of that tradition into the present day. The most interesting parts were the explanations of the relationship between Native and African-Americans. It's pointed out that Charley Patton's vocal style was derived from Native musical elements, and once you hear this, it can't be unheard even if the resemblance is coincidental. The New Orleans portion was fascinating, where we learn that part-Native people who could identify as black would do so to avoid being shipped off to a reservation, "because the Indians were treated even worse than the black people," and that Mardi Gras was welcomed as the only time when "black men could wear feathers." I would have appreciated more of this kind of ethnographic exposition, which is a different film entirely than "look, a Native American wrote this." However, the Native American contribution to popular music is one of its essential elements, and this documentary was long overdue.

history.title: In A Better World
history.text: In a world filled with violence--individual, gang, tribal, state; in a world of great disparity between what adults say and what adults do; in a world where mass shootings have become a daily reality but political leaders say the answer is more guns; in a world that tells us the state achieves security with a strong military and military action, while the best thing for individuals confronting violence is to turn the other cheek; and in a world where children see bullying every day as well as teachers who do nothing about it, it's no wonder that kids grow up wildly confused about violence and its place in our lives. Young schoolmates Christian and Elias are dealing with very big issues—divorce, death of a parent, and bullying at school and elsewhere. As the traumas big and small begin to add up, so does the anger, and the friends contemplate a violent response. In A Better World at first seems focused on the subject of violence and some of its undeniable truths, perhaps its inscrutability being the most undeniable of all. But the film ultimately and happily is not an analysis of the convoluted subject of the whys and whens of violence. It's much more interested in giving us a glimpse into the prism through which children witness violence and exploring the role we all play in shaping that prism. This is a visually rich film with a forceful screenplay that unfolds at a brisk pace. But its most enduring scene, one that the viewer finds very difficult to forget, is one of visual simplicity and involving the deeply profound lessons and legacy a parent can pass on to a child. It's a scene of poignant grace defined by a difficulty deliberately sought out, a challenge squarely faced, an indignity kindly overlooked, all for the selfless purpose of teaching an invaluable lesson to the most pliable among us … in order to make a better world. The relevance and humanity of this film are its exploration of how parents and other adults raise children in a world full of violence and what those adults teach—by word and by deed—about how to confront adversity and the urge to respond with violence. It's not always an easy film to watch despite the gorgeous cinematography. But the “emotional blows,” as one amazon reviewer writes, “are cleansing; as the characters work toward some kind of healing, so do you.” One leaves the theater “grateful for the experience.” At its most basic, this is a film about parents raising kids, and a beautiful reminder that you don't have to be a perfect parent. In an increasingly inexplicable world, for children and adults, you just have to have the courage and the wisdom—in word and deed—to be good enough.

history.title: Elephant in the Living Room
history.text: This project is quite a testament to the power of documentary cinema, introducing us to an intensely interesting story and intensely interesting characters--more compelling than almost anything found in most fictional film. Exotic animal ownership has become such a volatile topic that almost anyone focusing principally on one situation risks being accused of pronouncing judgment on the wider topic. But director Michael Webber tries, to the extent possible, to maintain objectivity and to steer clear of the wider pronouncement. Exotic animal owners have turned their cause into a civil rights issue. And traders, breeders, and profiteers have amplified that narrative to advance their own interests. On the one hand, as with gun ownership, that combination of circumstances produces a very undesirable situation in the U.S. On the other hand, the statistics prove that, left to government, industry, and the general public, some of the most majestic wild animals on earth will not be preserved and protected. Somewhere between species extinction and household ownership of exotic animals live a few soldiers whose job it is to try to make a bad situation as good as it can be. That's where this story takes place. And Webber couldn't have found a more compelling soldier than Tim Harrison--tough but empathetic, forceful but soft-spoken, highly complex but down-to-earth. Put him together with Terry, an intriguing animal owner in Ohio and his beautiful African lions, and you have a pensive documentary that always respects its characters and subject, as well as a wonder-filled story, worth watching and re-watching, that gives us all plenty of food for thought long after the film has ended. The Elephant in the Living Room thoughtfully explores proper placement of the line between wild animals and people. But make no mistake, this isn't a scholarly tome. The filmmakers will take you on an emotional journey that will shake you--at times pleasantly and at times not. Perhaps the most instructive part of that journey is realizing that, when trying to help animals, there is often emotional pain. And our protagonists must accept in this situation, as with life, that they can solve certain problems but must also learn to live with unsolved problems. Webber's selection of one problem-ridden case study could be (has been) criticized as advocating a position, but he also chooses not to address many problems common to owners, traders, and communities in the world of exotic animals. Ideologues on both sides may well interpret the film and its neutrality as hostility to their side. But Webber, despite slowly revealing a point of view, gives his viewers sufficient room to draw their own conclusions. One critic on this webpage, in addition to an excessive and ultra-biased critique, describes the human relationships portrayed in the story as cheesy. Tim and Terry may be imperfect individuals, but there's nothing remotely inauthentic or cheesy about either of them or the unlikely partnership that grows between the two. To fail to understand THAT is to miss a major component of the story and to show a deficit of insight into the human animal. This is a film about a true story; by definition, it's a documentary. One may not like the facts presented, but that in no way makes the film animal rights "propaganda."

history.title: Live In London [Blu-ray]
history.text: Here's a guy who's music is gorgeous and really goes deep emotionally. Just listen to Listen Without Prejudice or, especially, Patience. Those albums are tremendous listening experiences. A concert has the challenge of visually presenting that beautiful music with images that compliment, even enhance, the music. And a concert film then has to communicate those images. Alas, this film's visual communication is a massive distraction and only serves to detract from the musical experience. It's a mad, hyperbolic soup of bombastic light show, over-sized images, and, most regrettably, one long uninterrupted sequence, from show start to finish, of two-second shots. It's got to be one of the worse edited concert films I've ever seen. There's George, there's a backup singer, there's the audience, there's the light show, then the sequence repeats itself, over and over, in two-second cuts. A quarter of the way into the show, you're a little dizzy. Halfway through, your eyes start to hurt. At the three quarter mark, you have a headache and just want to watch something else. The film-makers are frantic, frenetic, maybe even manic, but definitely predictable and not imaginative. It's a live concert but, aside from a few brief moments, you won't see the musicians or their musicianship because the film-makers basically leave them out. Michael has still got a great voice, and when you're watching him you know you're seeing a born entertainer. All of the vocals are terrific as a matter of fact, but they have a tough time making their way through the film's visual haze. The special feature documentary is lighthearted but intimate, warm, enjoyable, and we briefly meet the band members. But if you really want to enjoy George's music, listen to his CDs. The guy is uber-talented ... obviously.

history.title: The Poseidon Adventure
history.text: Here is living, breathing proof that a film can be action-packed with special effects and still tell an absorbing and dramatic story--proof that action and hardware don't have to require that viewers check their brains at the door, and that films that do that are trite and lazy. Poseidon is about optimism and faith, leadership and sacrifice, living and dying, choice, and God's will for us. It doesn't get preachy and it doesn't get overly analytical. But it resonates with real ideas, real people, and a drama about how the two come together and how our protagonists hold on to hope against the backdrop of an escape from disaster. It takes the viewer on a visual journey not frequently traveled in the days before CGI, but it never forgets that the special effects are only the canvas upon which larger and more compelling ideas and emotions are painted. This was the "disaster film" that spawned the genre but contained none of the mind-numbing that became a hallmark of most of the films, driven by greed, that followed. Yes, Allen was a big part of those films. But the prototype, his masterpiece, held no promise of great wealth and was even nearly derailed over money concerns. Its production was driven by the things that make for great cinema and cinema lore: vision, ambition, smarts, an eminent director, top-notch screen writer, and a cast of seasoned Hollywood heavy-hitters who all deliver the goods. These folks act their hearts out--something to be genuinely savored considering that this caliber of performance won't be seen in any of the disaster films to follow. It's almost as if Poseidon really shouldn't be thought of as in the same category. And imagine that ... not a single firearm makes an appearance in this movie. No romantic visions of gun violence, no-one is shot, guns aren't pointed at people at every turn, and no-one barks those stupefying words, "Drop your weapon!" With all the action, the film-makers managed to make a thoughtful movie about the human condition that's lost none of its luster over the years and continues to deliver a positive message of hope: That in times of despair, we discover the inextricable link between courage and faith. It's not the fires and rising waters that are our adversaries; it's our fears and doubts. And it's often in the courage of others that we find our faith, our own courage, and our belief that "Life always matters very much."

history.title: Silver Linings Playbook
history.text: This is an amazing film that takes viewers on an emotional journey the way few films do. With an astonishing screenplay and incandescent performances, Silver Linings Playbook reaches deep down into emotional territory, compels us to do the same, and demands our unflinching attention when Tiffany exhorts, “That’s a feeling!” They say that actors inhabit characters, but that great actors allow characters to inhabit them. What a joy it is to watch these actors, at the top of their game, inhabited by rich, deeply developed, multidimensional characters full of joy and sadness, desire and dread, love and disdain, each contending in his own way with the inherent tug of war within between the tendency toward indifference and the aching desire for deep emotional experience—for a begrudging love of life in spite of it all. The film is a cornucopia of generously textured performances, but especially so with Cooper and Lawrence, who are heart-breaking and stunning in ways that can be difficult to convey in words—ways that reach down and touch an emotional core even for viewers who didn’t know they had one. And isn’t that what emotional recovery for all of us is really all about …. finding one’s emotional core and reactivating it. With Cooper and Lawrence, nothing more is required to break your heart than a simple facial expression, a movement of the eyes, or a brief action. There are microscopic moments in this film—when Pat hugs an unexpecting former employer, or when Tiffany locks flirtatious eyes on Pat and says, “Let’s go see the house.”—that embrace more tenderness and pathos than other pictures manage to capture in their entirely. If I were a filmmaker, Silver Linings would make me a very jealous one for sure. Is it a love story told against the backdrop of emotional recovery or a story of emotional recovery told against the backdrop of a love story? You decide. But there’s no denying that Silver Linings is a beautiful film about life’s joy and sorrow, and about a responsibility that each of us has … to face his own pain squarely … to go through the pain rather than be destroyed by it … to do the next hard thing … to create in each of our lives a silver lining. A famous man once wrote, “The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places.” But that only happens when the pain is transformed, by doing the next hard thing, into a road map to personal recovery, and hopefully with the support of family, friends, and professionals. Like Dr. Patel says to Pat: “The silver lining thing is yours [if you want it] … This crazy sad s*** as you call it made you a happier, calmer person with a beautiful positive philosophy of going outdoors, working out, and reading books.” To Dr. Patel and this magical collaboration of filmmakers, we respond: “Message received, loud and clear!”

history.title: The Damned United
history.text: This film is an embarrassment of riches: great true story, fantastic screenplay, amazing cast of actors, and an absolutely brilliant production design. Designer Eve Stewart is keen to capture the textures of the period—wood board construction, brick walls, chipping paint, solid wood furniture, wood paneling, busy wallpaper, wool tweed, and so much more. Did I mention wood. The viewer begins to look forward to Stewart's rich design walking into each scene, like a favorite cast character, and giving a warm embrace. DP Ben Smithard never passes up an opportunity to showcase England's famous natural environment—gray skies, cumulous clouds back-lit by the sun, the ubiquitous green foliage. The filmmakers want to transport you to that time and place, and they succeed mightily. This is a true story from the world of professional soccer in the 1960s and 70s, and there are a lot of elements that naturally propel a captivating tale like this. One of Tom Hooper's jobs is to stay out of the story's way. But his biggest challenge is portraying the relationship between Clough and Taylor. And this is where The Damned United doesn't fall into the usual trap whereby sports films try—and usually fail—to impart to the viewer the feelings of loyalty and affection that an entire team of players has towards a beloved coach. Hooper and screenwriter Morgan instead focus on the loyalty and affection between two men, and Sheen and Spall are flawless capturing the professional collaboration, the resonating emotions, and the personal imperfections as the two weather storms together. It's never cheesy, never sappy--always genuine, and very convincing. The production design's textures beautifully (intentionally?) compliment the textures of this relationship between two fascinating individuals. As one watches the relationship unfold, you feel you've been given a front row seat to the intimacies between two very close friends. And that's a very good seat to be in. Check out Morgan's excellent Frost/Nixon as well, also with Sheen.

history.title: Interiors
history.text: This film isn’t necessarily an easy one to watch, but that makes it no less pleasurable. It’s quiet, but not dreary … sullen, but not morbid. On the surface, it might appear to be an Allen diatribe against intellectuals and other tortured artists. But below that surface, it’s so much more. No, joyous isn’t a word that comes to mind when describing Interiors. And yes, it moves along quietly and is a heavily character-based story, with a number of its protagonists ultimately turning out to be decidedly unlikable. But when the film moves, it moves decisively. Through its quiet roars primal emotion. And with the exquisitely detailed fabric of its many varied characters is woven a brilliant story of family, loyalty, pain, love, and liberation; a story of mental illness and its effect on every family member; a story written by a man with wisdom apparently well beyond his years. Plot is sufficiently covered by other reviewers and essentially involves a mentally disordered woman, the struggle of her husband and three daughters to remain loyal over many years, and the emotional effect this all has on each. The daughters, all bright, in order to deal with their anxiety, and in at-that-time contemporary American fashion (almost nonexistent today), over-intellectualize things, cast doubt on their own qualities and strengths, constantly question the purpose of their lives, and generally make themselves miserable in the process. The husband, on the other hand, eventually confronts his dilemma through action—a decision to face his emotional turmoil, liberate himself from it, and do what gives him happiness in life. A new woman comes into his world, figuratively and literally breathing life and some semblance of joy into both the film and those characters who choose to receive her gifts. Though the film is always keenly focused on the daughters, it is through the father’s story that Allen communicates his thesis. That we do little to resolve our inherent anxieties by continuously questioning the purpose of our lives. In the short time we have on this earth, we have to act on life (not react to it), build our own purpose, define our daily living, and be present enough to enjoy the simple beauty and pleasure that life has to offer. A sick psyche is one thing—the real enemy is a “sick spirit.” The final scene on the beach is one of the most humanizing, deeply moving endings you’ll ever see in a film … dazzling. It’s such a beautiful, consuming, and haunting metaphor for Allen’s message that it shakes you a bit each time you watch it. If you’ve read other reviews on this site, you’ve been forewarned that some find this film “utterly depressing and gloomy,” with one unhappy reviewer thinking after watching the movie, “I’m going to get drunk and kill myself now.” But remember what Roger Ebert said: “No good movie is depressing, all bad movies are depressing." This is a good movie. And on an admittedly odd personal note, I tend to watch it over the holidays. It’s superbly acted, it has much to say about family life that many will relate to, and it delivers a very life-affirming message. Someone once criticized Allen’s movies for trying to tell people what they should already know. The reality of human nature is that positive messages have to be delivered over and over. And we should be grateful for a film like Interiors that delivers one … eloquently.

history.title: The Shipping News [DVD]
history.review_title: So Many Films, So Little Time
history.text: One amazon reviewer wrote of this movie, “ … if you read the novel by Annie Proulx, you'll probably be disappointed with the film.” Reading the novel is apparently not a requirement for being disappointed with this film. There’s little joy in writing a bad review, and this reviewer writes so few of them. It’s just that one expects that a film with this brilliant cast, and based on such a successful book, couldn’t possibly go wrong. But the expectation goes sorely unmet. A very prolific amazon reviewer put it into words that are so on-point, they’re worth repeating. “You'd think a story that includes [so many sobering topics] … might actually raise your pulse. But Robert Nelson Jacobs' screenplay is so resolutely inoffensive, and Lasse Hallstrom's direction so fatally cautious, that the film struggles to hold your attention … as it skips playfully over all that nasty stuff in hot pursuit of a fairytale ending.” The film-makers may have pulled together an impressive collection of film components, but they cannot “hide an empty core. You can't have light without darkness, you can't have growth without pain - and this film just doesn't have the nerve to go anywhere near either of them.” The story is about recovery from trauma, including the transformational pain that’s involved. But the message isn’t a particularly new one, leaving the film-makers with the responsibility of imparting to the audience compelling emotions--emotions that go beyond the message and that, for many people, are a necessary part of learning the idea behind the message. It's clear that quite a few amazon reviewers feel otherwise, but the superficial dialogue, the awkward performances, and (most importantly) the anemic recounting of the traumas in the pasts of these people, left this viewer feeling flat … and bored. There are many compelling films out there about this topic, so check out The Hours, Warm Springs, Silver Linings Playbook, The Prince of Tides, and many others. So many films, so little time.

history.title: Crash (Widescreen Edition)
history.text: The one thing this film’s detractors simply cannot abide, or forgive, is the auto wreck rescue scene with Matt Dillon and Thandie Newton. They either refuse to accept the officer’s ability to change bigoted attitudes the way he ostensibly does, or they’re too offended by what they see as the scene’s representation of black dependency on white benevolence. These are fair objections. But the refusal to question their assumption about inability to change is a prejudice all its own. Crash is a film about, more so than anything else, assumptions, and it asks everyone to question two assumptions, about anger and change, with wide-ranging implications for how people get along in the world. The common assumption about anger says that conflict among people, say racial conflict, triggers fear then anger. But here are some new premises to consider. Bear with me--there is a cinematic point here. There’s a school of thought that says “race” is a fabrication, a social construct, a piece of fiction created by the mind (to, say, rationalize subjugation). If one considers that there are virtually no biological differences among humans, that there’s only one human species, this thinking is correct. It’s also widely accepted in psychology that there is in life for most people a certain inherent anxiety, a persistent low intensity fear that compels us to look around for threats--an inheritance from thousands of years of evolution (an adaptive function), even if different people today experience that anxiety in different ways. It follows that perceived threats in the environment (say, for instance, different skin color) can easily trigger that anxiety, then the closely related emotion anger (“… anger is the subjective experience that accompanies aggressive impulses.” [Averill]), then aggression that may follow. In other words, people have a built-in anxiety that, in a sense, looks around for threats real or perceived. Racial difference turns out to be one of those threats, even if a social construct. The threat intensifies anger (in preparation for aggression). The anger produces conflict, even if the threat was a perceived one. So that racial conflict doesn’t precipitate anxiety and anger, even if it feels that way. But rather anxiety and anger predicate the construction of race and then precipitate racial conflict. It’s a massive corruption of the adaptive functions of these emotions, originally intended to keep us safe but now causing conflict. “Different” may seem to be the problem, but it’s really not. The problem isn’t on the outside, it’s on the inside--anxiety and anger. That’s the Crash. From anger that becomes crippling, the folks in this film are crashing into their own selves, and they’re forced to question their assumption about the origin of their anger … just as the film asks you to question yours. How Socratic! Crash involves racism, but it isn’t about racism. It’s about anger and change: recognizing the control anger has in our lives (like an addiction) and making a decision to change that, to give it up, to surrender it. All of the characters are dealing with an unbridled anger which they need to let go of before it destroys them. We may have to accept the inherent anxiety. But when the old way of being doesn’t work anymore, when there’s just too much pain, the anger can be changed, even if an emotional crisis is usually needed to do that. The inability for this kind of change is the second assumption the film asks you to question. And the film-makers are making their case that if we question the origin of our anger, we can let go of some of it, allowing people to change both themselves and the way they get along with others. There’s a spectacular heartbreak to the way these crises are portrayed, especially by Terrence Howard, who is unforgettable. And there’s a real artistry to this film that makes it a both exhilarating and thoughtful rendition of the transformative power of pain. Full of anguish, defiance, courage, humor, and beauty, Crash is a gorgeous, even if at times difficult, parable about change and hope. Twelve years after its release, it's clear its Best Picture Oscar was well deserved. The film may be a bit too much for some. But for others, it’s what cinema is all about! Roger Ebert wrote of this picture, “Not many films have the possibility of making their audiences better people.” But when art reaches deep into the viewer and touches both feeling and thought, that art can change people in ways that may last a lifetime. What nobler purpose is there of art. Crash is that kind of art. It acknowledges the mystery of life and, in portraying that mystery so elegantly, helps the viewer make peace with it. And wouldn’t we all eventually like to be able to say, in Pat Conroy’s beautiful words (from The Prince of Tides), “It is the mystery of life that sustains me now.”

history.title: Fahrenheit 451 [DVD]
history.review_title: For the Purpose of Being Human
history.text: This is a very capable adaptation of the novel, especially given the deteriorating relationship between director and screenwriter Truffaut and clunky, sometimes ineffective, lead Oskar Werner. Also complicating things was that an unbelievable wealth of ideas in the novel had to be mined very selectively to make the film. Nevertheless, Truffaut and his team made a sensitive, thought-provoking, and sometimes beautiful film that Bradbury greatly liked. There are three terrific special features on the DVD, and the novelist's participation in all of them is a highlight. Many of us read this book about a kinder gentler dictatorship long ago in high school or college, and it's sometimes hard to tell what's more frightening. That so much of the novel has come true, or that so many of the ugly things that have come to be in our modern, so-called civilized society (i.e., the internet, globalization, Big Data, corporate dictatorship) were beyond the imagination of even a great futurist writer. About so many things however, Bradbury was amazingly forward-thinking and spot on. His warnings about television, essentially now all but forgotten, were unreservedly prescient. He pulls no punches in exposing television (the “wall family”) for what it really is: a mind-numbing, anesthetizing fraud. There's a hilarious scene where the evening's TV entertainment is of two men having a manic, interminable conversation, struggling to cover the tiniest details, about the seating arrangement at an upcoming dinner party—in other words, about absolutely nothing … complete pointlessness. It all takes place on a big, wall-mounted flat screen, and everybody wants as many wall families in the home as he can afford. Sound familiar? It makes one recall Reynolds Price's line about the undergraduates coming into his classroom at Duke with their “poor television-devastated brains.” A few thoughts on how this writing genre got from there to here. In the wake of the horrific atrocities of two world wars in the 20th century, there emerged a “scientific” movement (social science, or behaviorism) with the benevolent aim of understanding causes of war, building a just society, and preventing appalling global conflicts. Two of the most famous isms to appear were socialism and communism. To achieve the mass cooperation needed for their version of widespread economic development, it was presumed that sophisticated methods for compliance with the “new doctrine” would be needed, such as shaping or controlling thought rather than using coercion. Around the world there grew enormous concerns that using science (generally used to understand physical realities) to create political systems (social realities) would produce an unwanted mutation—a new kind of dictatorship, a Frankenstein. Or maybe folks simply believed that all people of these isms were Godless savages. In any event, the fear was so intense that it influences anti-communism right up to the present day. At that time, a group of writers published quite a lot on the insidious methods of the new dystopia. In Bradbury's book, the government doesn't control people by controlling information through propaganda. It controls people through mass ignorance: drugs, television, and the banning of all printed words. Yup. It all seems a bit mad, and it begins to hit very close to home. But Bradbury and the film do maintain a sense of humor. Have some fun looking for the anachronisms, odd color schemes, and the film-makers' obvious disdain for modernist design (poor van der Rohe). There are also occasional brief shots, in a fully remastered film, shown unrestored. For those who think one would never see this kind of official misology in the modern world: When you see politicians, in the U.S. and elsewhere, rail against elites and their damnable ideas, the message is that knowledge will get you nowhere—exactly the government's position in Fahrenheit. You may not see state of the art special effects in this film, but expect a lot of food for thought of that sort. Bradbury once said that films today are brilliant technologically, “But you come out aching, and you’re hungry. You haven’t seen anything. With Truffaut, you've seen something.” The film’s thesis is clear and burning hot. The real threat is ignorance of thoughts and feelings, whether imposed by the few or freely chosen by the many. True, most people aren't interested in a lifetime of deep thinking, but the pendulum has swung too far in the opposite direction. It’s a bizarre irony that in a world of mass public education, there are so many people content to disconnect from books, plays, articles, poetry, all kinds of written words and the life-affirming thoughts and feelings, both positive and negative, that they contain—content to turn off leaning. And to disconnect from those thoughts and feelings is to disconnect from the two things that define what it means to be human in the most fundamental sense. When we disconnect from thoughts and feelings, we become intellectually and emotionally ignorant, we fail to understand self, and become disconnected from both self (alienated) and others (atomized). That’s the world of Fahrenheit 451, in some ways resembling our own world. So that it's not learning for some abstract elitist purpose. It's learning for the purpose of connecting with thoughts and feelings, both ours and those of others … for the purpose of being human. And in the end, that humanity (“simple human decency” [Chayefsky]) is all any of us really has in this life. Writers may be “a minority of undesirables crying out in the wilderness,” and they may write of pain. But pain reminds you that you're alive, and there can be no pleasure in life without it. Becoming comfortable with that reality--learning to cry as well as to laugh--is part of growing up. Literature is the “power of memory,” our history and future, and our collective thoughts and feelings. Remove it from your personal life, and those are the things likely lost. In Fahrenheit, this produces a mostly quiet, compliant, and self-absorbed public. In reality, we know that ignorance is at the heart of alienation, malice, and violence. Ultimately this isn't at all a story about what the government does. It's about the choices individuals make to remain connected, or not, to their humanness. Much of the film's visual bareness comes to an end in the final scene with the book people. It's one of those moments in cinema when imagery, music, screenplay, and performance--thought and feeling--come together to produce revelation … a sort of spirituality … and something with great pictorial and emotional beauty. Bradbury said, “If you have a good film and end it badly, you have a bad film. If you have a medium film and end it beautifully, you have a beautiful film.” The book people show us that Fahrenheit 451 is indeed a beautiful film.

history.review_title: Classic Peter Sellers Comedy Is A Must See If You Never Saw It
history.text: When this first came out in 1964, I laughed till my sides hurt. It was Peter Sellers second film as Inspector Clouseau, the bumbling detective, but the first one to feature him throughout. He was the inspiration for "Get Smart", Don Adams long running TV sitcom. While it is somewhat dated today, it still can make you laugh, and if you haven't seen it, it should really be hilarious. As with all comedy, it becomes less funny with repeated viewing, as the element of surprise is gone. Still, I wanted to add this to my DVD collection, as I think I laughed more on first viewing than any other film before or since.

history.text: This documentary seems too unbelievable to be true, but it is true. It is about an Anti-Semitic Austrian activist who discovers that his grandmother was a Jew, and thus by Jewish law, is himself, Jewish. Rather than denial, he decides to embrace Judaism and even gets a Bar Mitzvah and a Briss, eventually educating himself on the Holocaust by visiting Auschwitz. history.text: This was a big disappointment. Because I loved "The Scalphunters" in 1968, I figured I would like this film, as it has much of the same cast and production crew. But when I saw the name John Frankenheimer, I became wary, for while he made a couple of great films, most of his work was pedestrian IMO. This one was definitely in that category, where nothing about the film was convincing or particularly involving. The "savages" didn't seem savage enough, and the script was expository. After seeing it, and barely able to finish it, I realized why it is not one of Burt Lancaster's more well known films.
