history.review_title: Brilliant Portrayal of the Life and Times of Hugh Hefner
history.text: Once I started watching the first episode, I was hooked; couldn't stop watching until there was no more to watch. Although in many places I find it to be quite irritating, it remains as truthful and accurate as I can imagine a documentary series ever will be. This is a fast-paced, entertaining documentary about the life of Hugh Hefner and the story of the Playboy empire, with a great deal of its folly, some of its tragedy, all of its beauty, and most of its ugliness laid out with incredible frankness and honesty for all of us to learn from. There are a lot of very beautiful, naked women and even some R-rated sex, but nothing gratuitous there; the story of Hugh Hefner's life simply cannot be accurately depicted without those elements. Observations about the influence that Playboy had on the culture of the time might seem to be overly self-congratulatory, but within my experience, they are spot on. While it's tragic that rabid support for corrupt power-mad totalitarian politicians became inextricably entangled with Hefner's original quest for personal freedom, it's nevertheless true that Playboy was instrumental in communicating that odd mixture of philosophies to an entire generation of people who became the media moguls of today. I was there to watch these things happen. When Hefner started Playboy magazine, I was just 3 years old. I grew up as Playboy grew, so to a great extent, the events depicted in this documentary are the story of my life. In the voice-over at the beginning, Hef tells us that this the story of Playboy, "at least as I remember it." I can honestly say that, for good or for ill, the events are described are accurate as well as I remember, too. When I was 10 years, old, my family moved to Hef's home state of Illinois. I even graduated from the same school, the University of Illinois, albeit 23 years after he did. The continuing tragedy is that even to this day, Hefner has never realized that he actively supports the very things that he detests. His "women's movement" encounter should have taught Hefner that these politicos have no interest in the welfare of anyone but themselves--their only paradigm is their own personal power and their only tool is hate--and today you just need to turn on the television to see them still at work with the same one paradigm and the same one tool. Amusement for Hefner fans: I actually ran into Hef and his then-girlfriend Barbie Benton while I was at the University of Illinois. My first hint was in the morning. I'd been out flying at the Willard Field, the university's airport, and as I landed my little Piper airplane I saw that iconic black DC-9 aircraft with the bunny on the tail parked on the apron. The actual Hef sighting was a little later. Hef and Barbie were on their way into a bar called Stan's Gridiron while I was on my way out. Would it be unseemly for me to turn around and follow them back in, just for a bit of a gawk? Aw heck, nobody noticed me anyhow. Golly; Barbie Benton in the flesh. Oskee-wow-wow. I learned later that they were in town so that Barbie could pose for a local sculptor. Bumped into them again a few years later at the Johnson Space Center, where I was working and they were touring. Barbie was wearing a stretchy tube top when she tried on a space suit. To get into the top, you have to stretch your arms over your head, so... well... America's space program is mostly memories these days; some of those memories are more pleasant than others. We always remember close encounters with celebrities; that's one of the things that really distinguishes them as celebrities. Dick Gregory's description of the Chicago Playboy Club is spot on--the drinks were stiff and the food was great. I got my Playboy Card when I was 21 years old, and that place was a must-do on frequent visits to the Windy City. I don't even remember the menu on the buffet, but I do remember that it was mind-boggling. Ditto for the St. Louis Playboy club. Those were the days!

history.review_title: Low-budget portrayal of a long worn-out theme
history.text: A handful of quite good actors muddle their way through an unrealistic drama where the stereotypical British officer stereotypically orders his troops to commit suicide by attacking the German trenches, just like in movies about Gallipoli. It would be a wonder that the Brits could win the war with such incompetent officers, but the stereotypical German solders seem to be even more nuts. Meanwhile it's tragedy and angst all around when the pregnant wife back homes dies while trying to get an illegal abortion of some other man's baby. War is unpleasant, and WWI was especially nasty and pointless.

history.review_title: So bad it's an insult to the audience
history.text: "The Temple of Doom" is the movie that put me off Indiana Jones movies--so bad that I never again when to see one of the films in the theater. I watched it again in Amazon Prime to make sure and, yup, my memory serves me well. Despite its high budget and top-notch star, this is one of the worst movies ever made. We spent the entire time just wanting it to be over with. After it was released in theaters, we were not surprised to see that critics universally panned it. Yet, we see incredibly high ratings on Amazon. Easy to explain. At least now, based on the ratings and assuming they pay full price for the Amazon Prime accounts for their sock puppets, we can see that Disney spends at least $100, 000 per year for accounts to game the ratings, plus whatever they pay their writers for gushy reviews of movies they own. That's not a bad marketing investment considering that it's worth hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue.

"Moontrap Target Earth" was written by the same fellows who wrote the 1989 film, "Moontrap," Robert Dyke and Ted Ragsdale, and it shares the same basic idea of an advanced, ancient civilization that left dangerous robots behind. Beyond that, though, it's a far more cerebral treatment of the story (read: "low budget") and leaves a lot of open plot lines and unanswered questions. Nevertheless, even with its slow pace and unnecessary side shows, the film kept me interested and watching to the very end and proved to be thought-provoking enough to keep my mind going on it well afterward. [SPOILER] One scientific item of note: In the ending, the gizmo on the moon uses some super-duper science fictiony technology to terraform the moon. This is, in fact, quite reasonable if you can get enough atmospheric gasses to the moon in the first place. The moon's gravity is not sufficient to retain an atmosphere indefinitely, but if we were to somehow bring in enough oxygen and nitrogen to get Earth-normal pressure at the surface of the moon, and then do nothing to maintain it, it would take 10,000 years for the pressure to leak down by 1%. So, it's safe to conclude that if we had the ability to release that much gas the moon's surface, we would be able to maintain the atmosphere by slowly replenishing it. Water in the atmosphere would stabilize the surface temperature, and being a real "greenhouse gas" would probably trap enough heat to raise the mean temperature from -9F to something people can live in.

history.title: Now You See Me 2
history.review_title: Fine cast wasted on unnecessary, convoluted and ultimately tedious sequel
history.text: Directed by John Chu (G.I. Joe: Retaliation, Justin Bieber: Never Say Never) from a screenplay by Ed Solomon (Now You See Me, Men In Black), Now You See Me 2 is a considerable step down from the original Now You See Me. It's hard to know where to begin. With the exception of Isla Fisher, you have all of the great cast from the first movie plus the addition of a few other talented actors, and you have the writer of the original film as well, but this sequel is completely lacking in almost everything that made the first film work. For what it's worth, you will need to have seen the first film in order to make any sense of the sequel. But that said, seeing the first film will only help so much because the plot of the second is so convoluted and in many cases outright contradicting what was seen in the first film, for no other purpose that to try and make the need for the sequel seem credible. Trying and failing miserably. This film was a bad idea executed badly. About the only redeeming feature is the occasional bit of flash shown when the Horsemen perform, but even those pale in comparison to the flash shown in the original. Now You See Me 2 picks things up about a year after where the first film ended. The sole woman of the group, Henley Reeves, has apparently left the Four Horsemen for reasons that are just skimmed over. The remaining Horsemen - J. Daniel Atlas (Jesse Eisenberg), Merritt McKinney (Woody Harrelson) and Jack Wilder (Dave Franco) - have been in hiding, awaiting further instructions from The Eye, the secret society of magicians they were recruited into in the first film. Atlas, however, has gotten tired of just sitting around waiting, and has gone searching for The Eye himself. Which is kind of strange since the previous film had them supposedly finding The Eye and finding that FBI agent Dylan Rhodes (Mark Ruffalo) was a member of The Eye. But apparently Atlas is chafing at what he feels is Rhodes' leadership. Which we never see because Rhodes is still in the FBI and isn't doing anything with The Horsemen. Atlas's search leads him to an underground chamber where he an unseen voice that tells him that the Horsemen are about to see some action. Whereupon Rhodes enters the picture once again with a new mission: exposing corrupt businessman Owen Case (Ben Lamb), whose new software supposedly secretly collects data on its users for Case to exploit. Rhodes also introduces new Horseman Lula May (Lizzy Caplan), whom Atlas has already encountered, as the new member of the team to replace former member Henley Reeves. To reveal anything else would amount to potential spoilers. Which isn't saying a whole lot as a lot of the surprises and revelations take considerable suspension of disbelief, not to mention a willingness to just accept a lot of contradictions of what you learned from the first film. Which in turn don't really matter because you quit really caring long before the end of the film. Not really recommended unless you're seriously bored and have two hours to kill.

history.title: Lost Soul: the Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley's Island of Dr. Moreau [Blu-ray]
history.review_title: "Get me off of this insane island!" - Actor Rob Morrow to his agent
history.text: Written and directed by David Gregory (The Theater Bizarre, Texas Chainsaw Massacre: The Shocking Truth), Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley's Island of Dr. Moreau is a fascinating documentary of everything that went wrong with Stanley's notorious 1996 box-office bomb The Island of Dr. Moreau. The film ultimately cost some $40M to produce but its total lifetime gross box-office after 21 years is barely $49M, far short of what it would have needed to make a profit (roughly $100M in 1996 dollars or $156M in 2017 dollars). Actually, it's not fair to call it Richard Stanley's film as he was fired after barely a week or two after filming was supposed to begin. He was eventually replaced by John Frankenheimer (The Manchurian Candidate, The Train) after a number of other directors turned the job down due to the word-of-mouth about the project being plagued with problems. A lot of the documentary shows what Stanley originally had in mind for the film with storyboards and art, and it looks like a film that could have become a cult classic of the horror genre. Which the film that ultimately resulted is decidedly not. One note: Much as I liked watching it, I only gave this documentary 4 stars instead of 5 for two reasons. The first is that most of the documentary is about the early parts of the production where Stanley was involved and less dealt with the part of the production after Frankenheimer took over, making the documentary feel unbalanced. The second reasons is that Stanley has a very thick South African accent and a number of the other people involved had very thick Australian accents (it was filmed on location in Australia) which often made it hard to understand what was being said. Highly recommended for anyone who likes documentaries that show how and why some films become disasters.

history.review_title: "Save one person." "And then?" "And then you'll know."
history.text: Directed by Zach Snyder (Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice, Watchmen) and Joss Whedon (The Avengers, Buffy The Vampire Slayer) from a screenplay by Chris Terrio (Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice) and Whedon, Justice League may not be the best superhero team movie to date, but it's definitely one worth seeing, if only for the outstanding performances by Gal Gadot as Wonder Woman, Ezra Miller as The Flash, and especially Jason Momoa who actually makes Aquaman _cool_, The film starts with a prologue set in the very distant past, thousands of years ago, when an army of parademons from the world of Apokolips, commanded by an alien being named Steppenwolf (Ciarán Hinds) attempted to invade and conquer the Earth using the combined power of three objects called Mother Boxes. They were ultimately defeated by an alliance of Olympian Gods, Amazons, Atlanteans, humans, and Green Lanterns. After forcing Steppenwolf and his army to return to Apokolips, the Mother Boxes - now dormant - were taken and divided among the allies - the Amazons got one, the Atlanteans another, and the third was given to the humans - who hid them around the world. The film then moves back to the present, which picks up shortly after the end of Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice. Superman is dead and the world is in mourning. However the death of Superman has caused the Mother Boxes to reactivate and enable Steppenwolf's return to Earth to redeem himself with the master of Apokolips, Darkseid. Steppenwolf first strikes the Amazon home island of Themyscira and takes the first Mother Box. Queen Hippolyta (Connie Nielsen) sends a warning to her daughter, Diana Prince aka Wonder Woman (Gal Gadot) of Steppenwolf's return by lighting an ancient invasion signal fire. Diana meets up with Bruce Wayne aka Batman (Ben Affleck) and they set about trying to recruit the other "metahumans" he'd learned about in the previous film. Wayne first tries for Arthur Curry aka The Aquaman (Jason Momoa) but is rebuffed. He then meets up with Barry Allen aka The Flash (Ezra Miller) who gleefully signs up with fanboy enthusiasm, while Diana tries for Victor Stone aka Cyborg (Ray Fisher) who also declines. But both Curry and Stone ultimately join them, Curry after Atlantis is attacked and Stone after S.T.A.R. Labs is attacked and his father (Joe Morton) is abducted along with several other employees as part of Steppenwolf's efforts to locate and secure the other Mother Boxes. And thus the Justice League is formed. But whether they'll be able to withstand Steppenwolf's army and the power of the Mother Boxes is what makes up the rest of the story. There are admittedly some problems with Justice League as a film. While parts of it are truly great - mainly the action sequences of the various heroes as individuals and working together - other parts are uneven and feel somewhat disjointed, which is not surprising given the change of directors and the rather expensive re-writes and re-shoots that were done. But overall, the good parts outweigh the awkward or slow ones and Justice League is definitely worth catching, mainly for the performances. Gal Gadot brings the Wonder Woman action with the same intensity she showed in her solo film. Ezra Miller's Flash is every fanboy's dream of not only having superpowers but also getting to be part of the ultimate superhero team, but at the same time shows vulnerability and uncertainty, giving the film one of its best moments when Batman tells him what he needs to do. And Jason Momoa's Aquaman is nothing short of ground-breaking, taking a character that for decades was mostly a joke and making him not only cool but just plain awesome. Ray Fisher does a very creditable job as Cyborg, but he doesn't have enough screen time to give his character the development he needs. This is a case where the studio erred in not following the MCU model and giving his character a solo film before bringing the group together. Ben Affleck's Batman and Henry Cavill's Superman do have their moments, but for me was the other members that really made Justice League work as a film. The musical score by Danny Elfman is well done and really adds to the feel of the film, particularly as it occasionally works in the iconic themes from the earlier Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman movies. There are two credits scenes to watch for. The first one is just for fun, but the second one has a couple of important appearances that hold clues for the future of the series. Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys the action superhero genre.

history.review_title: Breath-takingly beautiful animated story of family, dreams and the things that bind us all together
history.text: Written and directed by Lee Unkrich (Toy Story 3, Finding Nemo) and Adrian Molina (The Good Dinosaur, Monsters University), Coco is a wonder to experience. Dazzling, breath-taking animation, marvelous story-telling, engaging characters and so much heart that it's a film that's going to stay with you for a long, long time. This isn't just the best animated film to come out this year, it's arguably the best film of any kind to come out this year. It's the first film in years that I immediately wanted to see again after it was done, like just not leave the theater and watch it all over again. It's that good. Coco takes place in Mexico on Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead) an important holiday in Mexican culture that is celebrated every year from October 31st to November 2nd (All Hallows' Eve, All Saints' Day, and All Souls' Day). Traditions connected with the holiday include building private altars called ofrendas where families display photos of those in the family who have passed on, often going back for generations, then honoring the deceased using calaveras (decorated skulls made of sugar), Aztec marigolds, and the favorite foods and beverages of the departed, and also visiting their graves with these as gifts. Visitors also leave possessions of the deceased at their graves. It helps to know this as background for the story, though the film does a good job of showing all of this as it goes on. It's all centered around the importance of family and of remembering those who have gone before you. Miguel Rivera (Anthony Gonzalez) is a 12-year-old boy who lives in a small rural village of Santa Cecilia with his elderly great-grandmother Coco (Ana Ofelia Murguía) and three generations of her descendants. Miguel's dream is to play the guitar someday, much like his hero, the famous Ernesto de la Cruz (Benjamin Bratt), a nationally celebrated musician and actor who came from his village and whose mausoleum is a major attraction there. However, there is a problem. Many years ago, Miguel's great-great-grandmother, the formidable matriarch Imelda (Alanna Ubach) was married to a musician who left her and their young daughter Coco to seek his fortune writing songs and playing music... and never returned. Imelda turned to shoe-making to support herself and her daughter, and eventually shoe-making became the family business. She also began a ban on any and all music in the family - no singing, no guitar-playing, no musicians! - which has continued to this day, rigidly enforced by Miguel's take-no-prisoners grandmother (Renee Victor). All of this serves as a major obstacle to Miguel and his dreams. Miguel does practice in secret though, watching old movies of the great Ernesto and teaching himself how to play, and decides in spite of everything to enter a talent show for the Day of the Dead. A sequence of events however result in Miguel stealing Ernesto's guitar from the mausoleum, and the next thing he knows is that he's suddenly an invisible ghost to the living - but the returning dead can see him and he can now see them. Which in turn sets him on a journey across a mystical bridge from the land of the living to the land of the dead, a wondrously beautiful place but one from which he must quickly find a way to return before he ends up becoming one of the dead himself and having to stay there forever. He's helped along the way by a down-on-his-luck denizen named Hector (Gael García Bernal), who's in danger of being forgotten, and a number of other characters he encounters. His quest ultimately requires him solving a generations-old mystery and setting right a wrong that occurred long before he was born. The musical score by Michael Giacchino (Up, Ratatouille) is as beautiful as the animation, shifting from lively to wistful as the scenes require, and young Anthony Gonzalez's singing voice gives heartfelt depth to Miguel's dreams of becoming a musician. Highly, highly recommended for anyone who loves animation, great story-telling and characters that grab you by the heart and never let go.

history.title: Goodbye Christopher Robin
history.review_title: Highly recommended for anyone who likes a story about how books ...
history.text: Directed by Simon Curtis (Woman in Gold, My Week With Marilyn) from a screenplay by Frank Cottrell Boyce (The Railway Man, Millions) and Simon Vaughn (A Bear Named Winnie), Goodbye Christopher Robin is the story behind A.A. Milne's classic children's story Winnie the Pooh. It's also the story of Milne's son - on whom the book's character Christopher Robin was based - and how that book became the bane of his existence. Highly recommended for anyone who likes a story about how books come to be and how they sometimes have unexpected effects on the lives of the people who inspire them.

history.title: The Man Who Invented Christmas(DVD)
history.review_title: Dickens: "The characters won’t do what I want. I’m the author here!" Scrooge: "Allegedly."
history.text: Directed by Bharat Nalluri (Miss Pettigrew Lives For A Day, MI-5) from a screenplay by Susan Coyne (Slings and Arrows, Anne of Green Gables) adapted from the book of the same name by Les Standiford, The Man Who Invented Christmas is an imaginative telling of how Charles Dickens came to write his classic novel A Christmas Carol. The performances by the cast are excellent, but two in particular stand out above the others: Christopher Plummer as Scrooge and Jonathan Pryce as Charles Dickens' charming but hopelessly irresponsible father, John Dickens. Note: it is absolutely vital that viewers have either read A Christmas Carol or at least seen a good film adaptation of it (the best IMHO being the 1951 version with Alistair Sim as Scrooge) before seeing The Man Who Invented Christmas. Otherwise they're going to miss most of the connections and references that occur in the film, particularly the more subtle ones dealing with where and how Dickens got his ideas for his characters. It is also helpful if viewers know something about Dickens' life, but the film does a fairly good job of filling in the background in that area. Highly, highly recommended for anyone who likes movies about the story-behind-the-story accounts of famous works, for anyone who's a fan of A Christmas Carol and/or Charles Dickens, and for any writer who's had to struggle with financial pressures, deadlines, writer's block and characters that refuse to do what you want them to do.

history.title: Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri
history.text: Written and directed by Martin McDonagh (Seven Psychopaths, In Bruges), Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri isn't what the trailers would lead you to expect. More than just a murder mystery/thriller, it's one of the most intricately written and directed films this year, a set of character studies brought to life in performances by an amazing ensemble cast. It's already received a number of awards and nominations including six Golden Globe nominations and is sure to be a contender in all of the major categories come Academy Awards time. In truth, the less you know about the plot, the more you're going to enjoy this film, because it keeps throwing curves at you, seldom doing what you expect but always keeping you thoroughly engaged. The set-up you probably already know from the movie trailers. Mildred Hayes (a magnificent Frances McDormand) rents three billboards on the outskirts of the small town of Ebbing, Missouri, asking the local sheriff, Bill Willoughby (an equally magnificent Woody Harrelson), why after seven months no arrests have been made in the case of the brutal rape and murder of her daughter, Angela (Kathryn Newton). This, as one would expect, sets a chain of events into action. But the twists and turns that chain takes and the revelations that come out as you go along are filled with the unexpected. Highly, highly recommended for anyone who loves a film that keeps doing the unexpected from beginning to end.

history.title: The Shape of Water
history.review_title: Giles: "It's not even human!" Elisa: "If we do nothing, neither are we."
history.text: Directed by Guillermo del Toro (Hellboy, Pan's Labyrinth) from a screenplay by del Toro and Vanessa Taylor (Game of Thrones, Everwood), The Shape of Water is, like so many of del Toro's films, in a category of its own. On the surface it's science fiction, but it's also a romance, a spy thriller and a character study. It helps if you're familiar with sci-fi films of the 1950's and early 60's, most particularly the 1954 classic film The Creature from the Black Lagoon. But this is The Creature from the Black Lagoon retold as a fantastically improbable love story, reminiscent in many ways of Spielberg's E.T. Set in the early 1960's, The Shape of Water begins at the secretive Occam Aerospace Research Center in Baltimore where Elisa Esposito (Sally Hawkins) works as part of the janitorial staff. Elisa is mute, the result of an injury sustained as an infant, but can hear just fine. She communicates by using American Sign Language, relying on her friend and fellow janitor Zelda (Octavia Spencer) to interpret for her to everyone else. Elisa lives in an apartment above a movie theater. Her neighbor and friend in the adjoining apartment is Giles, is a talented but struggling middle aged artist who is also closeted and gay. One day OARC the receives delivery of a strange creature in a water tank, captured by Colonel Richard Strickland (Michael Shannon) from a remote river in South America where the natives apparently worshipped it as some kind of river god. Strickland coldly refers to the creature as "the Asset" and "an affront" to God and nature. But Elisa sees the creature (Doug Jones) in very different ways, first with curiosity, then, as time goes on, with increasing empathy. Highly recommended.

history.title: Return of the Killer Shrews
history.review_title: with a precious few moments of decent acting from James Best. One of the often debated original film were ...
history.text: I am a huge fan of the original 'The Killer Shrews', and couldn't wait to see the sequel when I heard it was in production. 'Return of the Killer Shrews' is a big letdown. The whole film is taken as a big joke, with a precious few moments of decent acting from James Best. One of the often debated original film were the monsters. The 1959 shrews were created by covering dogs with monster suits. Some joke about it. It terrifies me. They move like real animals, fight with each other, jump at fences and mob fallen victims. No shrew suits ever fell off, and the dogs could move naturally & perform unhindered by their makeup. The CGI shrews in the sequel are in every way worse! They make CG effects in SyFy Channel films look like 'Avatar'. This movie lacks everything that made the original such a cult classic. My advice is to stay away from 'Return of the Killer Shrews' and treat yourself to the high-quality DVD from Genius Entertainment. This features both 'The Killer Shrews' and 'The Giant Gila Monster' restored to digital clarity with excellent colorized options included. ISBN # 1-5944-4709-8.

history.title: Icons of Sci-Fi: Toho Collection (The H-Man / Battle in Outer Space / Mothra)
history.review_title: if You Like Toho Monster Movies, You'll Love This Set!
history.text: Three classic Toho epics distributed in the US by Columbia Pictures. The most famous & familiar is 'Mothra'. Apart from her guest appearences in Godzilla movies, the fantastic being that is monster/goddess Mothra becomes manifest in this Tauburaya FX tour de force! The movie is entertaining & well acted. A must see! Fortunately, two more movies are included, as well 'Battle in Outer Space' and 'The H-Man' (aka 'Beauty and the Liquid People'). 'Battle in Outer Space' is a pseudo-sequel to 'The Mysterians', where Earth's new planetary defense force is pitted against the fiendish Natal. Amazing and new Tauburaya techniqes for urban carnage are introduced! Definitely a worthy successor to my beloved 'Mysterians'. 'The H Man' aka 'Beauty & the Liquid People' is a Police Drama confused by sci-fi crimes, as well as a super hot nightclub singer, Chikako Arai. Drug dealers, Cops, the underworld... are forced to deal with a scientist's conclusion that the source of all their problems is the gelatinous, highly radioactive, crew of a fishing boat that strayed into the waters of the Bikini H-Bomb tests. The acting is great, the effects are totally new & original from Tsuburaya, and the freighter's nighttime discovery of a ghost ship are not to be missed! For a very reasonable price, you get a trio of Toho's coolest, if lesser known, masterpieces. Get one while you can, before the price skyrockets!

history.review_title: 'Beginning of the End' is a Colossal Waste of Time & Money!
history.text: This movie scared me as a kid. It scares me more as an adult, knowing I wasted good money on the disc! Special effects are ridiculous! The worst being the giant locust swarm climbing the Wrigley Building. It's just a bunch of real, little grasshoppers walking on a photo of the historic building! At times, a few wander off & walk on the sky surrounding the building. The 1950s was an age of classic giant radioactive bug movies. This one sullies the rest. Go watch 'Them', 'Tarantula', 'The Black Scorpion' or 'Earth vs the Spider' for some legitimate multilegged scary fun!

history.review_title: This is no Gilmore Girls or Bunheads
history.text: For those of us who were expecting something along the lines of "Gilmore Girls" or "Bunheads," this is not it. This is more dramatic and dark than either of those shows. This has some similarities, such as a fast-talking and witty heroine, stiff parental figures who have a heart, fairy tale settings, and quirky characters. However, this one feels more personal and is less light hearted. I'm not sure what to make of it. It definitely has some darkness in it. Although pop culture references, music and dance were always a part of the Amy Sherman-Palladino shows, they were set in a current time. This one is set in 1958, and there are still lots of references to events and people of that time. What's weird is that each episode ends with modern music, even though the credits are set in a funky font from the 1950s or 1960s. There are some winning performances by Tony Shaloub, Alex Borstein, Kevin Pollack, Marin Hinkle and others. The lead, Rachel Brosnahan, is no slacker, but her character isn't as quirky as the female leads in "Gilmore Girls" or "Bunheads." I don't love it, and I don't hate it. However, it's not charming, which is what I was hoping it would be, since I was a fan of "Gilmore Girls" and "Bunheads."

I went into this not knowing what to expect. I was pleasantly surprised by how charming and moving this film is. It's not a depressing movie, which is what I was afraid of. It's warm, funny and thoughtful. It addresses family - what it is and what it means. It addresses how difficult it is to define yourself as a person who has a different plan than the plan your parents want for you. I have been a caregiver, and the hospital scenes were very realistic. You have to make a tough decision, and there's no time to consult with anyone. There's a lot of waiting around. There's a lot of trying to understand what all the doctors and medical professionals are telling you. There are a lot of emotional outbursts. There's constant uncertainty. There is a happy ending. Thankfully, this is no "Love Story." Thankfully, this is a movie that even non-millennials can enjoy. I'm not familiar with Kumail Nanjjani, but I'm assuming he brought a lot of his personal experience into this. He and Zoe Kazan seemed to have good chemistry. I know her from "Ruby Sparks," and just that. Holly Hunter is amazing - as always. Ray Romano surprised me with the depth he brought to his role. It was nice to watch a romance that wasn't saccharine or stupid.

history.text: Good but not great. It's like "The Graduate" for millennials. It tries SO HARD, and the music is horrible. There are some sound issues, and I had to hit the rewind button way too many times to make sense of mumbling actors. It's got a great cast, other than the young actor playing the lead. Very charming and filled with wonderful performances from Brenda Vaccaro, Dyan Cannon, Sally Kellerman and so many others. It's a romcom with a heart and it's smart. I wasn't sure what to expect since it us set in a retirement village, but it's funny, sweet and moving.

If these people were my "friends," I would find new friends. Then again, I am older than these whiny, self-involved Millennials. For the person who compared this to the "Big Chill," you are sadly mistaken. It's a bore. And the split screen shots didn't add to the story - they were a distraction. The shaky-cams was annoying. Yes, I get it. This is probably a low-budget indie film from a recent film school grad. What an absolute bore. Just because the characters scream at each other does not make it interesting or engaging.

history.review_title: Do not waste your time or your life watching this lame attempt at comedy
history.text: How could a movie with such a great cast be SO BAD? Because the script is SO BAD. This is a lame attempt at comedy. I cannot believe it's so bad. SPOILER ALERT: Here's the story: two parents decide to go on a cruise costing $3000 instead of participating in Christmas things that cost over $6000 because they are sad that their only child will be in Peru, serving in the Peace Corps - the first Christmas without the three of them. Then both of the parents get bullied by friends, coworkers, neighbors, and even their priest to participate in Xmas. What kind of person finds bullying funny? Social conformity is a form of bullying, and it's not funny - even back in 2004 when this movie was made. Then, their daughter calls to say she's coming home with her fiancee, so they decide to skip the cruise and go all in for Christmas with its ensuing "comedy." It's interesting that the Chicago suburbs have green, green grass in December - with snow on the ground, too. When the daughter's police escort is told to stall, it is a bit funny as the police car goes super slow and is passed by vehicle after vehicle. Then there's the party at the house with "hijinks" and a mystical Santa. Don't waste your time on this. There are far better classic holiday movies and even some modern day ones that are so much better. I don't think I'd want to hang out with people who find this movie entertaining. We obviously have a different definition of entertainment. So glad I watched this on Amazon Prime and didn't spend my hard earned money in a theater on this junk.

history.title: Sherlock: Season 3
history.review_title: Can you say self indulgent drivel?
history.text: I mean really, what happened? This show had everything going for it. I loved seasons 1 & 2. I had already pre-ordered season 3, I mean how could it not be great? Well, I just canceled that order. Episode 1 was OK, with some clever answers to how Sherlock survived. Episode 2 was so bad that I want that 90 minutes of my life back. I mean do I really care that Mrs. Hudson used to have great sex with her hubby, or that Molly is having great sex now? Plus Sherlock and John get drunk and make complete fools of themselves for what seems like half the show. This is the kind of crap that is on every network TV show in the U.S. It has replaced the fine writing that we saw in the first two seasons. Episode three was better then 2, but that really wouldn't take much. I may buy episode one on streaming video. It's the only one I really would care to watch again. Evidently the creators are aiming it all that the hormone driven fan girls and boys who can't wait for Sherlock to jump in the sack with somebody or anybody. Very sad.

history.title: Sherlock: The Abominable Bride [DVD]
history.review_title: The Adventure of the “Slow Brothers” SPOILERS!!
history.text: First let me start by saying that this series is what first got me interested in the character of Sherlock Holmes. The first and second seasons, while not perfect, were very enjoyable and I really like Cumberbatch as a modern day Sherlock. Sadly, with that said, I can’t help but say that this episode was terrible. It continued the downward spiral that began in season 3. Mr. Moffat and Mr. Gatiss say that they love the character of Sherlock Holmes. But although Cumberbatch has a lot of dialogue right out of Canon, the similarities seem to end there. The writers twist and turn Holmes into a drug addled looser who is only made great by Watson’s imagination. In fact, although Mycroft sometimes refers to Sherlock as “the slow one”, it turns out that both the Holmes boys are the slow ones, and Mary Watson, whether in the past or present is the smart one. While the Holmes brothers wander around in circles, Mary is busy uncovering a dangerous pro-suffrage group in the past and in the present, on her cell phone hacking into the government’s most secure websites without working up a sweat. Case closed. In truth, the first hour of the show was not too bad, with some clever dialogue. But even there you could see the feminist propaganda emerging and by the last half hour it was pure feminist crap. How very disappointing it was to see Sherlock made out to be a buffoon and to emphasize his drug use to such an extent that it was the basis for the whole episode. Obviously this episode along with season 3 were all made to please new generation of fan boys and girls who are more interested in everyone’s relationships and who everyone including Sherlock might sleep with, then a true mystery that only Sherlock Holmes can solve. I am sure that season 4 will only be more of the same. It’s sad to see this happening.

history.title: The Accountant (Blu-ray)
history.text: It is so nice to go to a movie and be surprised in a good way. This is what happened when I saw this movie for the first time. It is an action movie but it is so new and refreshing. No Political Correctness. You have two smart, strong women. Not the silly “macho” females that ruin almost every movie and every TV series these days. They are both great at their jobs and get things done. Ben Affleck has never been one of my favorite actors but this film moves him way up on my list. He really brought Christian Wolf to life and made him a complex and interesting character. Great action combined with just the right amount of humor and you have a Great Film. Sean Rowe’s song “To Leave Something Behind” that plays during the last scenes of the movie is icing on the cake.

Excellent movie. Was it perfect? No!. But in this age of Political Correctness it will probably be the best that we will ever see. The filming is beautiful and the romance between Tarzan and Jane is perfect. Even though the purists complain that Tarzan should have black hair and not blonde, I really thing these two are the Best Tarzan and Jane ever and there is a real chemistry between them.
Loved this movie. Mattew McConaughey is excellent as usual.

I’m glad to see so many positive reviews for this movie. When it came out it seemed that everyone hated it. True, this is not The Tarzan story that Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote. But is a fun re-imagining of that story. I am a life-long Tarzan fan and at 70 I have seen all the movies that are available and the TV shows too. I always try to find the good in every one of them. Except for the terrible recent series on Netflix I usually find something to enjoy. This movie was beautiful to watch. Loved the use of Parkour as Tarzan moved through the jungle. This is a great movie for kids too.
A nice documentary about the history of Tarzan. Lots of movie clips and commentary by Ron Ely, Christopher Lambert, Scott Tracy Griffin and many others. Check it out.

history.title: Spider-Man: Homecoming [Blu-ray] [3D Blu-ray]
history.review_title: Lots of fun, but nothing new
history.text: Spider-Man's back! Surely that's a statement that should have people much more excited, but after Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 2 the film franchise has gone on a steep decline. This is the second reboot of the web-swinger's motion picture adventures in less than a decade, and people are a bit tired because the quality of the latests films has ranged from mediocre to terrible. Does this movie return the franchise to enjoyable levels? Most definitely, just like The Force Awakens did for Star Wars. But just like that film, this one plays it too safe for its own good. Let's go over the positives first. Avoiding the pitfalls of The Amazing Spider-Man, this movie doesn't retread Sam Raimi's original film. Nor is an origin story in any capacity. This is good, because since this movie is set in the MCU alongside Iron Man, Dr. Strange and Thor all those superhero origin stories are starting to look the same. It's also a much more personal story rather than the last two films dealing with city-wide threats. In that respect it's a bit of fresh air. Then there's the whole deal with Spider-Man's suit being made by Tony Stark (aka Iron Man), which entails Peter Parker learning to use foreign tech he's not prepared to handle. The way the movie deals with Peter Parker is also really good. They show him having to juggle all his superhero responsibilities, highschool work and personal life stuff. It's also the first time where Peter Parker is correctly represented as a teenager, who looks and behaves like one. The villain is very well represented and wonderfully portrayed. On to the negatives, I feel like this movie doesn't really do anything special. There are a couple of surprising moments here and there but in general this feels more like a long episode of a TV series with more production values. The script just doesn't like to take risks. And while the movie handles Peter well, it doesn't do so great with Spidey. The fact that Spider-Man's suit has so much tech makes it feel less like Spider-Man and more like Iron Man Jr. And there's a problem from this film showing up so late in the MCU's life. Spider-Man used to stand out in Marvel comics for being a wise-cracker. But since pretty much every hero in the MCU is a jokester now, loving that ironic humor and sarcasm, Spidey feels like just another guy. It's one of the things that contributes to the film's generic feeling. The worst problem is Spider-Man's motivation. Yeah, it's great that they don't show us yet again Uncle Ben dying and all that, but that doesn't mean they should just remove the motivation. Spider-Man has always been about responsibility. Here, Spidey's entire motivation is to impress Tony Stark. Not only it makes it look less heroic, but also makes this move less about him. Tony Stark's physical presence in the film is short, but his influence spreads throughout the whole movie. Hell, even the villain is yet again a guy with a grudge against Stark (as if we didn't have enough of those in the Iron Man and Avengers movies). And I get that introducing diversity in films is a good thing, but could we please at least try to make it a bit realistic? One look at Peter Parker's group of friends and you'll expect them at any time to take out their rings and call Captain Planet. They look like a fast food chain commercial rather than a realistic group of friends. There's also a bit of excess humor. There are some genuinely funny moments, but others are predictable and annoying. I'd rather have quality over quantity. Now, make no mistake, the movie is a lot of fun, but there's nothing in it that will stay in you for days or even years after watching it. If you allow me to use a crude remark, this movie is like cranking one out: yeah, it's a fun way to pass the time, but it's not particularly memorable. Hopefully the next film in the franchise is able to shed away the fear of rejection and do its own thing.

history.title: DCU: Batman and Harley Quinn (BD)
history.text: Harley Quinn's popularity has risen well enough over the last few years that DC has put her everywhere to the point of annoyance, just like they did with, well, Batman. Considering this, it's strange that it took until this moment to make a movie in which they share title credit. Shame for Nightwing, though, who has a role just as large as any of them both yet the title completely ignores. Then again, after watching the film, maybe he asked his agent not to put this one on the résumé. As much as I believe both Batman and Harley Quinn are overused, I love both characters, so a movie about them was instantly interesting. The trailers did nothing for me, but they didn't look terrible, just uninteresting. Sadly, they turned out to be much more telling than I thought, because that's probably the best way to describe this movie: "not terrible, just uninteresting". Your mileage might vary, though. If you hate this movie, I'll understand. The obvious appeal of this film is the visual aspect, using the same art style from the classic DCAU Batman series, and some of the same voice cast. The movie doesn't explicitly state that it occurs in the same continuity (and if it does, there are a couple of continuity problems with it), but on the surface it looks like an extended episode of the series. Kevin Conroy and Loren Lester are back as Batman and Nightwing, and for them these roles are like putting back a comfortable pair of pajama pants. They slip in effortlessly. Less lucky is Melissa Rauch (who you might know as Bernadette from The Big Bang Theory) as Harley Quinn. While Rauch has a natural voice that fits the character perfectly, here she's instead trying an imitation of original voice actress Arleen Sorkin, which feels terribly forced and sounds excruciatingly grating. The plot is as follows: Batman foe Poison Ivy teams up with similarly plant-themed creature and relatively obscure DC villain the Floronic Man in order to find the formula that transformed scientist Alec Holland into similarly plant-themed less-obscure-but-still-not-very-famous DC "hero" Swamp Thing, and use it to transform all of Earth's living beings into plant life. Batman is forced to recruit the help of Ivy's friend Harley Quinn in order to locate her before she can put her plan into action. Hijinks ensue. If you're a fan of the Batman animated series this movie is based on, you'll recognize that this is pretty much the exact same plot as the one from episode "Harlequinade" (Season 2, Episode 7), only replacing Joker with Ivy and adding Nightwing for good measure, so no points for originality. The way the story develops is less than ideal as well, with too many unnecessary, long scenes added just for the sake of a joke or two. The padding is obvious, and it's clear that the plot of a 22-min episode it's not enough to fill a 74-min movie. Worse, while this movie (seemingly) forms part of the DCAU, it expects you to have extensive knowledge about characters that have never been introduced in it until now. If you happen, for instance, to know nothing about Swamp Thing coming here, prepare to be swamped (tee hee). But fine, you can claim that the story is merely an excuse to get these characters together. How do they fare? Not very well, I say. While at moments the characters feel well like themselves, more than once they simply change personality in order to make others look different or just for (again) the sake of a joke. If you've ever seen a Michael Bay movie you'll know what I'm talking about. Characters just don't feel cohesive enough. And let's not even get to the ending scene, which is an exercise in insulting both the audience and the characters. Which brings me to the worst part: the humor. Now, the Batman animated series (and the entire DCAU in general) had a great handling on humor. The writers made sure it fit. You wouldn't have Batman cracking a joke about sexy girls just like you wouldn't have Flash pretending to threaten a criminal with a deadly disease only to reveal it was just water all along. The humor in this movie is TERRIBLE. It's Adam Sandler quality. Did you expect to live your whole life knowing that there'd never be a Batman movie with fart jokes? Well, I'm sorry to inform you that even if you die tomorrow, that ship has already sailed. From the very beginning, the Pink-Panther-movie-like intro credits are a massive red flag but trust me, you won't be prepared for just how bad it gets. All in all, I can't recommend this movie, unless maybe you're a diehard fand of the Floronic Man, who's the only character that doesn't get thoroughly trashed. It gets points for Bruce Timm's classic visual style, most of the voice acting and some of the action scenes, but the rest is uninteresting at best and rage-inducing at worst. Unexplicably, the writer for this movie, James Krieg, has worked in the excellent Green Lantern animated series, Batman: the Brave and the Bold and 90's Spider-Man animated series. He can clearly craft a good story, so I don't know what happened. Executive meddling would be my guess. "Make it more kid-friendly" (which it most certainly isn't, by the way), "Make it funnier", "Do this", "Do that". Just another victim of someone with lots of power and zero talent overtaking those in the opposite position. A shame.

I never watched the previous live-action incarnation of The Tick. I've only sporadically taken a look at the cartoon and I've sampled very few of the comics, but I understand what The Tick is about. It has been ingrained in me like Star Trek, The Godfather or other movies or shows that I've only watched long after pop culture made them familiar to me, despite its relative obscurity. That's why I wasn't enthusiastic by the trailer. It looked like it couldn't decide on a tone, and the humor (very important for the character) seemed lacking. I still decided to watch the pilot, and I'm glad I did, because I was instantly hooked. While not as over-the-top ridiculous as previous incarnations, this series takes a slightly more realistic approach (or rather, sticks the title character in a somewhat realistic world), but the series doesn't suffer for it. In fact, it's probably one of its biggest strengths, as it help us relate all the more to the main character, as he finds himself suddenly thrust into insanity. The real protagonist of the series is Arthur, a mild-mannered guy who suffers from PTSD after witnessing the death of his father and favorite team of superheroes at the hand of supervillain The Terror. The world believes The Terror is dead, killed at the hand of major superhero Superian, but Arthur knows better and he's determined to prove it, well against the wishes of his protective sister. In the middle of investigating criminal smuggling a technological powersuit, he's suddenly made the target of a friendly stalking by an unknown and outlandish superhero called The Tick, who's determined to prove Arthur that his destiny is to become a hero. Finding himself unwillingly wearing the suit, Arthur is now the target of the criminal organization and needs to figure out if he wants to come back to his old complicated but familiar life or embrace the call of heroism. While Arthur is the protagonist, the titular character is the star. The Tick is sane but wacky, strange but heroic and annoying but well-intentioned. While he never reachs camera-winking levels of 4th-wall breaking like, say, Deadpool does, he's a bit self-referential and seemingly more aware of the rules of storytelling than about his own existence. He really is a lot of fun, but a lot of his humor depends on context and that's likely to be the reason why the trailer didn't interest me. All of the characters are great and wonderfully portrayed, but the main two easily steal the show, The Tick with his wackiness and Arthur with his emotional backstory. This is a series that deserves to go on for longer, and I hope it does, because I want more of it.

history.title: Arrow: The Complete Fifth Season [Blu-ray]
history.text: Seasons 3 and 4 of Arrow were pretty divisive. Even those who liked them had to admit there were aspects of them that didn't fit together and as a result there was a lot of disjointed episodes and both seasons suffered from characterization issues. The showrunners realized they had to do something if they intended to win the audience back, and they did: it's called Arrow Season 5. A real back to form for the series, it's just as good as the first two seasons. Oliver Queen is the new mayor of Star City, and now has to reconcile these responsibilities with his night job as the Green Arrow. The events of the last season have made him wonder if he did the wrong thing by taking a non-lethal approach to crime fighting, and this decision coupled with personal issues and responsibilities from other members of his team have caused a split up. Now Oliver finds himself training a new team to fight crime while a new crime boss is taking the place of the last one. Meanwhile, a new villain peeks on the horizon. Someone with a personal grudge against the Green Arrow and working in the shadows to test Oliver like he's never been tested before. It's important to mention that the major problem with the last two seasons was the relationship plot tumor. The writing seemed more focused on finding new ways to make Oliver have relationship issues than in advancing the plot, and both the story and characters suffered in consequence. A secondary problem was that the classic flashback subplots were stretched far beyond need, spending several episodes to solve something that should take only one. Both of these were corrected in this season. Relationships now don't take focus away from the plot, characters are not forced to behave in ridiculous ways just to create conflict and the flashbacks are well crafted. Acting is better than ever. In particular Stephen Amell does his best work to date and the villain is simply astonishing. The story is well crafted as well, and leaving aside a couple of episodes that deal with personal issues or a crossover between all DC CW shows, the plot advances with good pacing. If next season is half as good as this one it'll still be great. A note aside, because I see some silly reviews complaining: yes, there's an episode dealing with gun control. But no, it's not propaganda from whatever side. It presents the issue as one that's not easily solved and doesn't really take any sides. Ignore the ramblers, the show is here to tell a story, not to sell political propaganda.

history.title: The Flash: The Complete Third Season [Blu-ray]
history.text: A spin-off from Arrow, The Flash started out with a spectacular first season that raised the stakes for superhero TV shows. Second season was just as good for most of its running time, faltering a bit at the end (including a severe drop in writing quality in a particular episode). Hopes were still high for third season, Seeing how those few quality drops were the exception and not the rule. Sadly, they seem to be the new rule. It's not a bad show by any means, but it feels like going back to the "Lois and Clark " time. A time where continuity wasn't a priority and characters would act as the plot demanded rather than how their personalities did. That worked back then, but in 2017 this is not one, but several steps back. The consequences of Season 2's finale left Barry Allen in a bad emotional shape. Not being able to stand the pain, Barry traveled back in time to stop his mother's death (the event that kickstarted his careers as both a forensic investigator and The Flash), creating a new life for himself. Taking cues from the event that inspired this season's plotline, "Flashpoint", Barry finds himself dealing with the consequences of his meddling with the timeline slowly robbing him of his powers and memories. While he manages to "repair" the timeline, cracks start to show up and Barry realizes he's now created a new enemy for himself, a speedster named Savitar, who has a personal crused against Barry and intends to ruin his life. Time travel is always a complicated subject, and rules are hard to keep track of. Even in the first two seasons of this show, the rules have been shaky, but it was forgiven because the writing was good. But here, the complete and utter lack of respect for continuity reaches frustrating levels. The entire arc of the season only starts because writers ignore the rules established by the previous two and then proceed to further mangle them well beyond recognition. For instance, Barry has an ally from a parallel universe who has to hide his face due to his version in this universe being a known criminal, and at some point he's found giving a public lecture with his face well on display on several pictures, and no explanation is offered as to why people forgot this guy's a wanted criminal. But even when not dealing with time travel the writing is poor quality. The plot only happens because everyone acts like a fool. Heroes seem unable to learn their lessons and keep comitting the same mistakes. Characterization comes and goes. Some characters are not given their due and others are given too much despite not needing it. Some adaptations of popular villains from the comics are devoid from all what makes them interesting. But the worst part, without any shadow of a doubt, is the main villain of the season. He's boring, uninteresting, and visually unappealing. It's only in the last few episodes when they inject a little characterization on him, yet he never even reaches the level of one-note monster-of-the-week, despite being a season-spanning villain. It says a lot when the most interesting villain of this season is actually the major antagonist on another show. Make no mistake, it's still a fun show. It has its touches of good writing, nice action scenes and the acting ranges from adequate to great (particularly Tom Cavannagh, who's just as exceptional here as he was in the previous two seasons). The problem is that the issues are so prominent that they keep preventing you from partaking in that fun. Here's hoping the show doesn't have to wait until its fifth season to come back to its greatness like Arrow did.

history.title: Transformers: The Last Knight
history.review_title: An instant classi... HAHAHA, no, but seriously, it's fun if you know what you're expecting.
history.text: Look, at this point in this franchise, you already know what you're gonna get. You either like these movies or you don't. If you're expecting to suddenly start liking them, that's not gonna happen. On the flip side, I see a bunch of reviews from people who claim to have liked the previous ones but dislike this one. While not altogether an unlikely claim, the reasoning some people are giving is suspect, as this movie doesn't fail in ways the previous ones didn't. Everything you can claim this movie does bad was already present in the earlier entries, and sometimes it was even more blatant. I have a... complicated relationship with these movies. I understand they're bad (the first one being the only one I can legitimately call "decent"), I do not think they're "misunderstood", but I still like them. I still find enjoyment in watching them, for whatever reason I've never really bothered to dig up. Maybe I already know to go with low standards, maybe I find a deeper appreciation for the subtle storytelling that occurs way below the in-your-face loud screaming and explosions, maybe I just really like to see giant robots fight each other. It doesn't matter, the point is that I'm gonna review this film for what it is and not for what it should be because, again, at this point, it's what we have, and it's pointless to expect anything different as long as the same hands are in charge. And for what this movie franchise is, this is a pretty good entry in the series. The trailers would let you believe that the major plot of the movie is to have the Autobots fight a brainwashed Optimus Prime. In reality, that barely qualifies as a C-plot and it ends almost as soon as it starts. A bit dissapointing but not entirely unexpected. The real plot of the film is that the Decepticons are hunting for an old Transformer relic that will help them revive their old planet, Cybertron while, of course, the Autobots are trying to prevent it with the help of a group of humans who've been secretly working with Transformers for centuries. Meanwhile, tensions between humans and Transformers haven't really improved much since the events of the previous film (which, for a series that doesn't really do much in the way of continuity, surprisingly makes a lot of sense). At the other side of the universe, the alien creature responsible for the creation of Cybertron has brainwashed Optimus Prime and sends him in search of the relic. All of this culminates in a race against time in order to find and destroy the relic before Cybertron is fixed by sacrificing Earth (very much like in the events of the third film). So yeah, that's the plot. Nothing original and the climax is perhaps too similar to that of Dark of the Moon, but it's serviceable. The plot retcons events and ideas from the previous films here and there but that's nothing new. Acting is decent and visuals range from spectacular to "I have no idea what's going on", and dialogue ranges from "Oh, that's neat" to "Please, for the love of God, shut your mouth and never, ever open it again", so nothing new there either. Some truly emotional moments are underscored by preposterous writing that should entirely ruin them, but the performances are good enough that it doesn't, because the actors are putting the effort that the writers refuse to. Well, some of them anyway. There are more than a few continuity nods and gags about Transformers in other media, which should bring a smile to some people. In conclusion: it's a Michael Bay Transformers movie. Nothing more, nothing less. If you liked the previous ones, chances are you're gonna like this one. If you didn't like the previous ones, this one will do nothing to change your mind. While seen just as a movie this would earn a 1 and 1/2 star rating at most, as a Michael Bay Transformers movie it easily earns 4 stars.

history.title: Alien: Covenant
history.review_title: Watch only if you're interested in seeing Michael Fassbender making out with himself
history.text: Alien is a franchise made popular by its two first movies, which curiously belong to different genres. The first one is pretty much a horror film while the second one is action focused. Both of them are great and beloved for different reasons, showing that this is a franchise that works well in different approaches, even if the basic plot is similar. Unfortunately, later sequels have failed to take advantage of this and their quality has suffered due to poor writing. After a couple of crossovers with the Predator franchise, they decided to come back to basics making a prequel, Prometheus. Divisive as that film is, it does succeed of pulling the old trick by focusing on sci-fi this time. Alien: Covenant, a movie which is both a sequel to Prometheus and a prequel to the original Alien, unfortunately, can't decide what genre it wants to belong to. This is, sadly, the least of its problems. The movie suffers from terrible writing, terrible characterization and a complete lack of focus. The only reason this isn't the worst movie of the franchise is the existence of Alien vs Predator: Requiem. Though since that movie isn't considered canon, this one might as well take the title. The plot goes like this: a ship named The Covenant is traveling to a far world with the intention of colonizing a new planet. Out of sheer coincidence, they run into a distress signal, which they follow to a world that looks habitable for humans and decide to investigate. Proving that government-sanctioned employees are just as dumb and useless in the future as they are today, they explore the place unprotected, leading to a couple of them becoming infected by parasites that explode out of their bodies into Neomorphs (the precursors to Xenomorphs), who give them chase to a point where they're rescued by David, the android from Prometheus. He then proceeds to experiment with them in the guise of helping them in order to perfect the Xenomorph species, finally answering the question that literally no one was asking, Ridley Scott: how did the Aliens came to be? Here's the major problem with this film: it takes everything that's bad about all the previous ones and almost nothing that's good. The descent into cheap horror cliches from Resurrection and Requiem? It's here. The mentally challenged crew from Prometheus? It's here. The complete lack of tension from AvP? It's here. The lack of characterization from almost every movie after Alien 3? It's here. The excess CGI that has plagued the series since the third film, making some of the creatures painfully un-scary? It's here. Wanna know what's NOT here? Everything the end of Prometheus hinted at. Rather than building onto what that film ended on, they decided to just shove that aside and follow an entirely different path, effectively making Prometheus entirely pointless, which is a shame, because despite its problems (some of them very serious), it's a far superior film to this one. In the process of trying to fix the issues with that film they created a far worse one in almost every aspect. The few positives are as such: the movie looks beautiful, mostly. Leaving aside some grating CGI here and there, the visuals are gorgeous. Acting is mostly good, with Michael Fassbender being the clear standout, particularly considering he's playing two characters this time. And, I don't know, I guess I should give them props for the fact that Ridley Scott didn't come into my house to personally use my Blu-Ray collection of Alien movies as toilet paper. As a sci-fi, horror or action film this completely and utterly fails. As an Alien movie, it's frankly insulting. I can only recommend it to the most die-hard Michael Fassbender fans. Everyone else avoid even if you have to kiss a facehugger to do so.

No spoilers. Star Wars was at a crossroads after the divisive "Episode VII: The Force Awakens". That movie was a hit, but it was also accused of being too similar to "A New Hope", and rightly so, since it did rehashed many of that film's story beats and ideas. But, ultimately, it was understandable, as after the unpopularity of the prequels Disney decided to play it safe with the start of their new trilogy, and at least people were looking out to the next films expanding upon the new ideas and mysteries set by TFA. So now they needed to make a decision. Will the next movie play it safe too or take risks? After watching it, it seems they tried to do both, and they stumbled. "The Last Jedi" will probably end up being even more divisive than the previous film. This movie does not follow the same beats of the equivalent "The Empire Strikes Back", but it does take cues and similar ideas from other Star Wars movies, particularly "Return of the Jedi". But, in general, it does try new stuff, and it pays off in the sense that it feels original, but not in the sense that it feels unsatisfying. Ideas range from "Interesting" to "Why? Why in the world would you do that?" and story beats go from shocking to predictable. While TFA was directed by J. J. Abrams, TLJ is directed by Rian Johnson, and this man seems to take his job as a new president who's dead set in erasing away all the changes done by the previous administrations, whether those were good or bad. If you were excited for all of those ideas and mysteries TFA left, prepare to be dissapointed as literally every one of them gets changed, destroyed or outright ignored. If you were the kind of fan who got a kick of making theories about what could happen, prepare to throw those theories to the Sarlacc Pit. Yes, you'll most likely be surprised, but that doesn't mean it'll be in a good way. Most of the time it's better to be predictable than dissapointing. The most noticeable thing is that this movie doesn't really feel that much like Star Wars. Leaving aside Rey's personal subplots with Luke Skywalker and Kylo Ren, the rest of the film feels more inspired by Star Wars than an actual part of it. The stakes are there, but the scale isn't. There are a few interesting visuals in one of the (very) few planets visited, but that's it. This is particularly noticeable in Finn's subplot, which looks like it belongs to an entirely different film. There are a couple of new characters, none of which are even remotely interesting, and some of the older ones suffer from bad characterization. The ones coming from TFA are properly treated, though, particularly Rey and Kylo Ren, who get more fleshed out and oughta get more fans on their side because of it. There's also a cameo by a popular character that's neat to see and will probably bring a smile to your face, but it's unnecessary and frankly counterproductive to another character's development. A couple new creatures show up as well, and they're nothing interesting. If you were excited about porgs, I'll warn you that calling them a footnote in this film is doing them a favor. Visually speaking, this film is absolutely gorgeous, so it has that going for it. The score is as good as always, but nothing new stands out. All in all, it's an entertaining film, but only an average Star Wars movie. Unlike Rogue One, it has characters you care about. Unlike TFA, it has an original storyline. Unlike the prequels, it's not saddled with complicated politics and silly visuals. But in trying to avoid those old pitfalls it runs into entirely different ones. I recommend not to watch any previous Star Wars films right before seeing this movie, since you're more likely to appreciate it if you don't have the previous ones in mind. Unless, of course, you never watched them, in which case it's absolutely necessary.

history.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past (The Rogue Cut)
history.review_title: The best version of this film, but not a must-have
history.text: X-Men: Days of Future Past is one of the best comic book movies in existence. It has great action, tension, characterization, a well-crafted and perfectly paced storyline and amazing visuals and scoring. I was a bit scared for this cut, since I felt it might ruin the film's pacing, but luckily, my fears didn't pan out. This is the definitive version of the film. That being said, it is only ever so slightly, so unless you're a completionist or really curious, if you already have the theatrical version of the film, this one is practically unnecessary. The plot of the film isn't changed, but the extra scenes add some interesting bits of story and characterization that fit the tone of the film and help the movie feel more cohesive. They also address a couple of minimal plot holes from the original, though sadly they still don't bother to explain stuff that left casual audiences confused, such as Professor Xavier's return after his death in X-Men III (which was addressed elsewhere) and Kitty Pride's new, unexplained consciousness-time-travel powers (which were never addressed). There are also a couple of new extras that are far more interesting that the ones included in the original version, so that's definitely a plus. The one thing that puzzles me, though, is the decision to call this extended edition "The Rogue Cut". Yeah, Rogue is there now, but her screen time is absolutely minimal and her role in the film ends up largely unjustified (she's supposed to be there to replace Kitty Pride after she's injured, but the movie never makes it look necessary by, saying, having Kitty die from her injuries at some point later). So yeah, if you don't already own any version of the movie, this is the one to go, but if you do own the theatrical version it's certainly not a priority.

history.title: Justice League: Throne of Atlantis (Blu-ray)
history.text: "Justice League: Throne of Atlantis" is the sequel to "Justice League: War", the third DC DTV movie from the New 52-based films kickstarted by "The Flashpoint Paradox". After DC rebooted their comics universe with their New 52 imprint they decided to do the same with their animated movies. The reception has been more or less the same in both media: lukewarm but still managing to attract a lot of audience. Regarding quality, it's generally mediocre, and this is no exception. This is the consequence of having this new series of films being directly adapted from stories from the comics rather than merely inspired by them, and the comics are generally mediocre. While I haven't read the comic this movie is based on, I've read other Aquaman comics from the New 52 imprint, and it's apparent that this movie doesn't do the characters any favors. The storyline for this movie is a largely watered-down version of the Justice League episode "The Enemy Below". While there's gore here where there wasn't in the animated series, characterization is far weaker, which is a bad thing, considering the basic plot (man tries to kill family to inherit the throne and do as he pleases with the kingdom) is extremely derivative. The Justice League episode made up for that with amazing character arcs and fun action, but this movie lacks in both departments. Most characters feel like caricatures of their originals, if not outright useless. In fact, Aquaman pretty much feels like less than a secondary character in what's arguably his own movie. The story also suffers from bad pacing, having most of the running time dedicated to setup and things only really starting to move along way past the halfway point, then ending abruptly. Then there are the subplots, which are just as weak. There's the bit about the Justice League not being sure if they're an actual team or not, which is mentioned once and never again brought up. The same happens with Batman's reluctance to be part of the group, which last about ten seconds. There's still the romance between Superman and Wonder Woman that no fan in history was ever invested in. There's even an eliminated sequence seen on the extras regarding Batman's investigation on Scarecrow. The sequence is short (less than a minute), but feels entirely pointless and it would have ruined the pacing of the film even further if included. Speaking of extras, these are definitely the highlight of the disc. There are a few features on DC underwater villains, a Comic Con panel, the film's score and, as usual, four included episodes from DC's cartoons, all of them associated to Aquaman, and all of them far more fun and interesting than the movie. So, if you're a completionist, go for it when it's cheap. Otherwise, avoid. It does nothing new or interesting and your time is best spent watching something else.

history.title: Fushigi Yugi Eikoden
